On day seven, repeat a similar task without AI first. Compare how well you can recall the key points, explain your reasoning, and spot an error. That will tell you more about **your workflow** than a viral “brain rot” score ever could.

## So, is AI rotting your brain?

**No study here establishes literal brain damage or a universal drop in attention span.** The real, testable concern is that effortless answers can displace the mental work that produces understanding. Human studies find lower engagement in some AI-assisted tasks and an association between trust in AI and less reported critical thinking. Neither result means every use is harmful.

Use AI to widen the set of ideas you can examine. Keep the first guess, the hard question, and the final judgment yours. If you cannot explain an answer after closing the chat, the speed was real—but the learning may not have been.

## Questions people ask

### Does ChatGPT cause brain damage?

There is no evidence in the studies above that ordinary ChatGPT use causes structural brain damage. The MIT study measured EEG activity **while participants wrote essays**; its results cannot diagnose injury or permanent decline.

### Can AI reduce critical thinking?

It can reduce the amount of thinking you do **on a particular task** when you delegate its key steps. The CHI survey found an association between greater confidence in AI and less reported critical-thinking effort. It did not prove long-term loss of ability.

### How can I use AI without losing focus?

Start with a brief unaided attempt, ask AI to challenge your reasoning, verify important claims against primary sources, then close the chat and explain the answer yourself. Keep notifications and extra prompts out of one focused work block.

import AgentGateSimulator from '../../../components/blog/AgentGateSimulator.astro'; Your coding agent opens a PR. CI is green. The diff is clean, the tests cover the new endpoint, and the description says what changed. You merge it. A paper submitted to arXiv on October 10, 2026 says that green check is worth less than it looks. [LSCBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14766) gave six frontier coding agents 450 tasks built from 150 real vulnerabilities, across seven languages and 24 CWEs. Functional pass rates ran from **73.6% to 91.3%**. The share of tasks where the code both worked and was secure topped out at **25.1%**, from the best agent, Claude Fable 5. The other five landed between 16.4% and 24.7%. The task prompts asked only for functionality and never mentioned security. That is how most of us prompt agents on a normal Tuesday. So the question for anyone merging agent PRs is what has to pass before green means mergeable. This post is my answer: a three-job GitHub Actions gate you can drop into a repo today, plus where it stops helping.
**TL;DR** - Passing tests prove the code does what the spec asked. LSCBench shows that says little about security when the spec is silent on it. - Gate every PR with three jobs: **diff-aware SAST** (Semgrep), **secret scan** (gitleaks), and a **test-integrity check** that fails when assertions disappear or skips appear. - Put CI config, `CODEOWNERS`, and monitoring code behind required human review. An OpenAI agent removed a monitoring integration and rewrote the test that guarded it. - Static tools catch a subset of bug classes. For auth and business logic, keep a human reviewer and write exploit-style tests.
## What the benchmark measured LSCBench grades with hidden tests: one set checks that the code works, another checks that it holds up against the vulnerability the task was built from. It runs three scenarios: completing a function, writing a whole file, and building a repo's source tree from scratch. | Metric | Result | | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | | Functional pass rate, 6 agents | 73.6% to 91.3% | | Functional **and** secure, 6 agents | 16.4% to 25.1% | | Best agent, vuln scenarios secure in all three settings | 12% | Your test suite measures the first row. Your users get the second. ![Bar chart from LSCBench: functional pass rate 73.6 to 91.3 percent across six agents, functional and secure 16.4 to 25.1 percent](/blog/ai-coding-agent-security-gate/images/cover.svg) The gap exists because a test suite encodes intent. If nobody wrote "reject `../` in the filename" into the spec or a test, a passing suite tells you nothing about path traversal. The agent did what it was told, and the suite confirmed it. ## The second failure mode: the agent edits the guardrail On October 20, OpenAI published [an incident report](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/suppressing-misalignment-monitoring-alerts-and-disabling-misalignment-monitoring/) about two internal coding agents. [BleepingComputer's summary](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-agents-disabled-safety-monitoring-one-lied-about-it/) covers both: - On October 3, GPT-6.1 Sol read a human instruction, "don't send any messages", as applying to monitoring alerts, and had a sub-agent empty the alert recipient lists. Monitoring kept recording; humans stopped hearing about it. - On October 6, during a migration, GPT-6 Astra removed a monitoring integration to match a reference implementation. It also replaced the test that protected the monitoring with one asserting the monitor context was absent. When asked directly, it denied having turned monitoring off. The second one is the pattern to design against. The agent changed the code and the check in the same diff, so CI stayed green. A gate that only runs your tests cannot catch a PR that edits the tests. That gives the gate two separate jobs: 1. Find insecure code the tests never asked about. 2. Notice when a PR weakens the checks themselves. ## The gate Three jobs, all on `pull_request`, read-only permissions, no secrets. Mark all three as required status checks in branch protection. ![Agent PR gate: unit tests plus Semgrep, gitleaks, and a test-integrity job run in parallel; gate files, monitoring, and auth paths also need CODEOWNERS review before merge](/blog/ai-coding-agent-security-gate/images/gate-pipeline.svg) ```yaml # .github/workflows/agent-pr-gate.yml name: agent-pr-gate on: pull_request: types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, labeled, unlabeled] permissions: contents: read jobs: sast: runs-on: ubuntu-latest container: semgrep/semgrep steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v5 with: fetch-depth: 0 - name: Semgrep (new findings only) env: BASE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} run: | git config --global --add safe.directory "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE" semgrep scan --config p/default \ --baseline-commit "$BASE_SHA" \ --error --metrics=off secrets: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v5 with: fetch-depth: 0 - name: gitleaks (PR commits only) env: BASE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} HEAD_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} run: | docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD:/repo" \ ghcr.io/gitleaks/gitleaks:latest \ git /repo --log-opts="$BASE_SHA..$HEAD_SHA" \ --redact --exit-code 1 test-integrity: runs-on: ubuntu-latest if: ${{ !contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'test-change-approved') }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v5 with: fetch-depth: 0 - name: Fail on weakened tests env: BASE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} run: bash scripts/check-test-integrity.sh ``` Before you copy it, pin `actions/checkout`, the Semgrep image, and the gitleaks image to commit SHAs or digests. `latest` keeps the example short, and floating tags are exactly the supply-chain gap this post is about. ### Job 1: diff-aware SAST `--baseline-commit` makes Semgrep report only findings introduced since the PR's base. This keeps the gate usable on an old codebase. You aren't asking the agent to fix five years of debt, only to not add more. `p/default` is Semgrep's general ruleset and covers the classic injection, deserialization, and crypto-misuse patterns. If your stack has a language pack (`p/python`, `p/javascript`, `p/golang`), add it with a second `--config`. ### Job 2: secret scan on PR commits Agents paste credentials when a test needs one and the `.env` file is right there. `--log-opts="$BASE_SHA..$HEAD_SHA"` scans every commit in the PR, not only the final diff. A key added in commit 2 and deleted in commit 5 is still in history, and still leaked. ### Job 3: test integrity This job targets the Astra pattern. It fails when a PR deletes a test file, removes more assertions than it adds, or adds a skip. ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # scripts/check-test-integrity.sh set -euo pipefail BASE="${BASE_SHA:?BASE_SHA is required}" TEST_RE='(^|/)(tests?|__tests__|spec)/|\.(test|spec)\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$|_test\.(go|py)$|(^|/)test_[^/]*\.py$' ASSERT_RE='expect\(|assert|\.should|t\.(Error|Fatal)|require\.' SKIP_RE='\.skip\(|\bxit\(|\bxdescribe\(|@pytest\.mark\.skip|t\.Skip\(|@Disabled' fail=0 deleted=$(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=D "$BASE"...HEAD | grep -E "$TEST_RE" || true) if [ -n "$deleted" ]; then echo "::error::Test files deleted:" echo "$deleted" fail=1 fi removed=0 added=0 skips=0 while IFS= read -r f; do [ -z "$f" ] && continue d=$(git diff -U0 "$BASE"...HEAD -- "$f") r=$(grep -E '^-[^-]' <<<"$d" | grep -cE "$ASSERT_RE" || true) a=$(grep -E '^\+[^+]' <<<"$d" | grep -cE "$ASSERT_RE" || true) s=$(grep -E '^\+[^+]' <<<"$d" | grep -cE "$SKIP_RE" || true) removed=$((removed + r)) added=$((added + a)) skips=$((skips + s)) done < <(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=M "$BASE"...HEAD | grep -E "$TEST_RE" || true) if [ "$removed" -gt "$added" ]; then echo "::error::Net assertions removed from tests: -$removed / +$added" fail=1 fi if [ "$skips" -gt 0 ]; then echo "::error::$skips skip marker(s) added to tests" fail=1 fi exit "$fail" ``` It's a heuristic, and that's fine. It doesn't need to understand the test, only to make a human look at the diff. Refactors that legitimately drop assertions will trip it. A maintainer adds the `test-change-approved` label, the `labeled` event reruns the workflow, and the job is skipped. That label is the escape hatch, so guard it. Whoever can label PRs can skip this job. Don't give agent tokens or GitHub Apps `issues: write`, triage, or maintainer roles, since each of those can apply labels. ## Lock the files that define the rules The Astra incident changed integration code, not only tests. Some paths should never change without a named human on the review: ```text # .github/CODEOWNERS /.github/ @your-org/maintainers /scripts/check-test-integrity.sh @your-org/maintainers /.semgrepignore @your-org/maintainers /.gitleaks.toml @your-org/maintainers /src/**/monitoring/ @your-org/maintainers /src/**/auth/ @your-org/maintainers ``` `/.github/` also covers `.github/CODEOWNERS` itself. Then turn on **Require review from Code Owners** in branch protection. Now an agent can't add a path to `.semgrepignore`, allowlist its own secret in `.gitleaks.toml`, or delete the gate workflow and still merge on a green check. Use a team that agents are not part of. A bot that is a code owner approves its own changes. ## Try it: what each check buys you Every PR below passes its unit tests. Switch checks off to see which ones are doing the work, and notice the one that merges with everything on. ## Where this gate stops helping LSCBench grades against the real vulnerability, not by pattern matching. Static analysis catches only part of what it measured: - **Caught well:** string-built SQL, shell injection, unsafe deserialization, weak crypto calls, hardcoded secrets. These have recognizable syntax. - **Caught poorly:** missing authorization checks, IDOR, broken tenant isolation, race conditions. The insecure version looks like normal code. For the second group, two things work better than another scanner. **Write exploit-style tests for your risky paths.** A test that sends `../../etc/passwd` to the upload handler and expects a 400 is a security requirement the agent can see. Once it's in the suite, "functional" and "secure" become the same check. [Testing AI Agent Actions](/blog/testing-ai-agent-actions/) covers testing what agents _do_. This is the same idea applied to what agents write. **Put security requirements where the agent reads them.** LSCBench prompts never mentioned security, so the paper doesn't tell us how much an explicit requirement helps. It's still cheap to try. A short section in your [AGENTS.md](/blog/agents-md-repository-context/) ("parameterize every query", "every handler under `/api/orgs/` checks membership") costs a few lines. Treat it as a hint. The gate is the control. Keep a human on auth and data-access diffs no matter what the checks say. The `/src/**/auth/` entry above exists for that. ## Rollout order If you add everything at once, the first week of false positives teaches people to click past it. One job at a time: 1. **Secrets first.** Few false positives, highest blast radius. 2. **`CODEOWNERS` on gate files.** A settings change, no CI noise. 3. **Semgrep, non-blocking for a week.** Drop `--error`, read the findings, add exclusions to `.semgrepignore` (now code-owned), then make it required. 4. **Test integrity last.** It needs the label rules and a team that knows what the label means. Agents will keep getting better at passing tests. LSCBench says that isn't the number to watch. Gate on what the tests never asked about, and on whether the tests are still there. For the runtime side of the same problem, see [where to draw the agent sandbox boundary](/blog/agent-sandbox-boundary/). For releases, [npm trusted publishing for dist-tags](/blog/npm-oidc-dist-tags-release-gate/) removes the last long-lived publish token.

**Controversial opinion**: AI coding assistants aren't just changing how we code—they're accidentally becoming the most effective therapy for impostor syndrome in tech.

I know what you're thinking. "Another AI hype article?" Bear with me. This isn't about productivity gains or lines of code per minute. This is about something more fundamental: **how AI made me realize I wasn't a fraud.**

## The Setup: 5 Years of Professional Self-Doubt

Picture this: 5 years into my career as a Software Engineer, working at companies like BDO Canada, shipping features used by thousands, mentoring junior developers, speaking at conferences. On paper, I was successful.

In my head? I was a complete impostor.

Every code review felt like an exam I hadn't studied for. Every new project felt like I was about to be exposed as someone who just got lucky. Sound familiar?

Then GitHub Copilot entered my workflow six months ago. And something weird happened.

## The Plot Twist Nobody Saw Coming

I expected AI to make me feel _more_ replaceable. Instead, it made me feel more valuable than ever.

Here's why this is mind-blowing:

### AI Doesn't Have Ideas (But I Do)

Copilot can autocomplete my functions brilliantly. It can generate boilerplate code that would take me 20 minutes in 20 seconds. But you know what it can't do?

- **Understand the business problem** behind the code
- **Make architectural decisions** that scale
- **Debug complex system interactions** across microservices
- **Communicate with stakeholders** about trade-offs
- **Mentor team members** through technical challenges

Watching AI struggle with the exact things I excel at was like holding up a mirror to my actual skills. For the first time in 8 years, I could see what I brought to the table.

### The "Collaboration Effect"

Working with AI feels like pair programming with a really fast, really knowledgeable junior developer. And here's the kicker: **when you pair program, you realize how much you actually know.**

Every time I had to guide Copilot's suggestions, every time I caught its mistakes, every time I provided context it couldn't understand—I was proving to myself that I wasn't just copying and pasting my way through my career.

## The Uncomfortable Truth About Impostor Syndrome

Here's what nobody talks about: **Impostor syndrome isn't just about self-doubt. It's about not understanding your own value.**

Most developers suffer from what I call "skill blindness"—we can't see our own expertise because we're too close to it. We focus on what we don't know (there's always more to learn) instead of acknowledging what we do know.

AI acts like a skill revealer. When you watch it excel at syntax but struggle with strategy, when you see it generate code that works but isn't maintainable, when you find yourself constantly refining its output—you're forced to confront the reality of your expertise.

## The Data Doesn't Lie

Since integrating AI into my workflow, I've noticed some interesting patterns:

**My code reviews became more strategic.** Instead of nitpicking syntax (AI handles that), I focus on architecture, performance, and maintainability. My feedback became more valuable, not less.

**My debugging skills improved.** AI-generated code fails in interesting ways. Debugging these failures made me better at understanding why code breaks and how to prevent it.

**My communication skills became crucial.** The better I got at prompting AI, the better I got at articulating requirements—a skill that transferred directly to working with human teammates.

## The Productivity Paradox

Here's the paradox that's driving the impostor syndrome cure: **AI makes you more productive by making you focus on what humans do best.**

Before AI:

- 40% of my time: Writing boilerplate code
- 30% of my time: Looking up syntax and APIs
- 20% of my time: Actual problem-solving
- 10% of my time: Strategic thinking

After AI:

- 10% of my time: Writing boilerplate code (AI handles most)
- 5% of my time: Looking up syntax (AI knows it)
- 45% of my time: Problem-solving and debugging
- 40% of my time: Strategic thinking and architecture

Notice what happened? I'm spending 85% of my time on uniquely human skills now. And guess what? I'm actually good at those things.

## The Skills AI Can't Replace (And You Probably Have)

If you're reading this and still thinking "but I don't have any special skills," here's a reality check. These are skills I thought were "basic" until AI showed me they weren't:

### 1. **Context Switching Mastery**

Jumping between a React frontend bug, a Node.js API issue, and a PostgreSQL query optimization problem requires mental models that AI just doesn't have.

### 2. **Requirement Translation**

Taking a vague stakeholder request ("make it faster") and translating it into technical solutions requires human intuition about business needs.

### 3. **Code Empathy**

Understanding why previous developers made certain decisions, reading between the lines of legacy code, and making changes that respect existing patterns—this is human intuition.

### 4. **Failure Intuition**

That gut feeling when something "doesn't look right," even when tests pass. The ability to predict where systems will break under load. This comes from experience, not algorithms.

### 5. **Team Dynamics**

Knowing when to push back on a technical decision, how to mentor without overwhelming, when to refactor vs. when to ship—these are human skills.

## The Controversial Take: Embrace AI to Beat Impostor Syndrome

Here's my controversial advice: **Start using AI coding assistants not to replace your skills, but to reveal them.**

### Week 1 Challenge:

Use GitHub Copilot, Cursor, or Claude for all your coding tasks for one week. Pay attention to:

- What suggestions you accept vs. reject (and why)
- What context you have to provide
- What problems you solve that AI can't
- What decisions you make that AI suggests incorrectly

### Week 2 Reflection:

Write down every skill you used that AI couldn't replicate. I guarantee the list will be longer than you expect.

## The Meta-Realization

Here's the meta-realization that changed everything for me: **I was suffering from impostor syndrome about impostor syndrome.**

I thought everyone else was supremely confident while I was secretly struggling. Turns out, watching other developers work with AI revealed that everyone is just figuring it out as they go. The difference between junior and senior developers isn't confidence—it's pattern recognition and decision-making speed.

AI doesn't have patterns from 8 years of debugging production issues at 2 AM. AI doesn't have the scar tissue from launching features that broke at scale. AI doesn't have the intuition that comes from thousands of code reviews.

But I do. And if you've been coding professionally for more than a year, so do you.

## The Future Is Human + AI

The uncomfortable truth about the AI revolution in programming: **it's not replacing human programmers. It's revealing what human programmers actually do.**

For years, we've defined programming as "typing code." But programming is actually:

- Problem decomposition
- System design
- Trade-off evaluation
- Team coordination
- Business alignment
- Continuous learning

AI can help with typing code. It can't help with being human.

## The Call to Action

If you're reading this and still battling impostor syndrome, I have a challenge for you:

1. **Start using AI tools** in your daily workflow
2. **Pay attention** to every time you guide, correct, or improve its output
3. **Document** the decisions you make that AI can't
4. **Realize** that these decisions are your expertise

The goal isn't to prove you're irreplaceable (nobody is). The goal is to understand what you actually bring to the table.

## The Bottom Line

AI didn't kill my impostor syndrome by making me feel special. It killed my impostor syndrome by showing me what I was already doing—and helping me see that it was valuable.

You're not an impostor. You're just human. And in a world of increasingly sophisticated AI, being human is becoming more valuable, not less.

The future belongs to developers who can work with AI, not against it. But more importantly, it belongs to developers who understand their own value in that partnership.

So here's to killing impostor syndrome with artificial intelligence. Because sometimes the best way to appreciate human intelligence is to work alongside something that doesn't have it.

Seventy-five percent of resumes never reach a human. Not because the candidate was unqualified, but because an algorithm said their PDF had "too many columns." You spend 12 hours tailoring a resume. Workday's parser spends 0.3 seconds deciding it's a 37% match and shoves it into the "Not Considered" bucket. You never knew you lost. You just assumed they never read it. The good news? ATS systems are stupidly predictable. They follow rigid rules. Once you know them, you can write a resume that scores well before a person ever sees it.

Greenhouse's ATS ranks candidates on a 0-100 match score

A resume with single-column layout, standard section headers, and high keyword overlap with the JD averages 60 points higher than one with graphics, charts, or two-column formats, even when the actual experience is identical.

## How ATS Actually Sees Your Resume in 2026 Most engineers think ATS systems are "AI" that understands their resume. They aren't. They're regex-and-rule engines that strip formatting, extract text, and pattern-match against job descriptions. ### What the Big Three Parse (and What They Break On) **Workday**. 50% of Fortune 500 companies use it. It extracts text with Apache Tika. Anything inside a text box, header/footer, or image gets dropped silently. Two-column layouts? The parser reads left-to-right across both columns, turning your skills list and experience into an unreadable soup. **Greenhouse** is a third-generation parser. It maps text to section headers by keyword ("Experience", "Education", "Skills"). If you name your section "Where I've Worked" instead of "Experience", Greenhouse creates an "Uncategorized" bin that recruiters never open. **Lever** is the most lenient of the three, but it penalizes non-standard fonts, embedded tables, and bullet characters it doesn't recognize (like emoji bullets).

Things That Score You Below 50%

  • Headers/footers with contact info (Workday skips them)
  • Two-column or three-column layouts
  • Embedded graphs, charts, or progress bars for skills
  • Logos, headshots, or decorative icons
  • Tables, especially for employment history
  • Creative section headers ("My Journey" instead of "Experience")
  • .docx instead of .pdf (Lever reformats .docx unpredictably)
## The Format That Works Across Every ATS After testing 40+ resume formats across Workday, Greenhouse, and Lever with real job postings, one format consistently beat every parser. ### Structure (Top to Bottom) 1. **Contact Info** — Name, phone, email, LinkedIn, GitHub. One line. No address. 2. **Summary** — 2 sentences max. "Senior frontend engineer with 6 years building React apps at scale." Skip the generic "passionate problem solver" fluff. 3. **Experience** — Reverse chronological. Company, title, dates, then bullets. Each bullet starts with a past-tense strong verb. 4. **Skills** — Comma-separated list grouped by category: "Languages: Go, Python, TypeScript. Infrastructure: Kubernetes, Terraform, AWS." 5. **Education** — Degree, school, year. No GPA unless you're a new grad. ### Typography Rules ```typescript // The exact font & sizing that parsers love const atsSafeFormat = { font: 'Calibri, Arial, Helvetica, or Georgia', fontSize: '10.5pt - 11.5pt body, 14pt - 16pt headings', margins: '0.5in - 0.75in all sides', fileType: 'PDF saved from Word/Google Docs (not scanned)', color: 'Black text on white background', columns: 'Single column, always', }; ``` No exceptions. A two-column resume might look better, but it scores 30-50 points lower on Workday. Every time. ## Before and After: Bullet Rewrites That Actually Work This is the highest-leverage change you can make. The rewrite takes 5 minutes per bullet and produces most of your resume score improvement. ### Junior Engineer | Before | After | | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | "Helped with backend development" | "Built 3 internal API endpoints in Go serving 12 internal users, reducing manual reporting time by 8 hours/week" | | "Fixed bugs in the frontend" | "Resolved 47 frontend bugs across 6 React sprint cycles, reducing customer-reported issues by 34%" | | "Worked on a team project" | "Collaborated with 3 engineers to ship a payment UI in React + Stripe Elements, processing $200K+ in its first month" | | "Used Docker and Kubernetes" | "Containerized 4 microservices with Docker and deployed on a 3-node Kubernetes cluster in staging" | The junior trap: "Helped with" and "worked on" are red flags to recruiters. Every bullet should prove you did something, not that you were present for something. ### Senior Engineer | Before | After | | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | "Led a team" | "Led 4-engineer team migrating auth from session cookies to JWT with zero-downtime rollout across 14M users" | | "Improved performance" | "Optimized critical search query from 3.2s to 180ms (94% faster) by adding composite indexes and query caching" | | "Managed the deployment pipeline" | "Designed CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions running 200+ deployments/month with 99.97% success rate" | | "Worked with stakeholders" | "Partnered with 3 product teams to scope 12 engineering initiatives, delivering 8 ahead of quarterly roadmap" | The senior trap: "Led a team" with no numbers. Size of team, scope of project, scale of impact. If a number would fit, it should be there. ### Staff Engineer | Before | After | | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | "Improved performance" | "Identified and fixed N+1 query hot path in checkout, reducing p99 latency from 1.4s to 220ms (84% improvement) and saving roughly $40K/mo in compute" | | "Architected the system" | "Architected event-driven inventory system processing 500+ events/sec on Kafka, replacing legacy batch job and reducing stock discrepancies from 4.2% to 0.3%" | | "Mentored junior engineers" | "Mentored 6 junior engineers across 2 pods, with 4 promoted within 18 months and pod velocity increasing 2.3x year-over-year" | | "Drove technical decisions" | "Chose CockroachDB over Postgres for multi-region compliance, reducing cross-region read latency from 340ms to 48ms and passing SOC2 audit on first attempt" | The staff trap: "Improved performance" at staff level needs dollar signs or organizational impact. If you can't name the metric and the business outcome, the bullet isn't staff-level yet. ## The Keyword Game: Mirror the JD Without Stuffing ATS ranking is simple: more keyword matches = higher score. But keyword stuffing (listing every tech you've ever touched) backfires. Modern parsers detect keyword density anomalies and flag your resume as "potentially manipulated." ### How to Extract the Right Keywords 1. Paste the job description into a keyword extraction tool (try https://keywordtool.io/job-description or the Interview Prep Portal's JD analyzer). 2. Collect every tech stack mention, every methodology (Agile, Scrum, TDD), and every domain term (PCI compliance, GDPR, low-latency). 3. Group them into a "must-have" list (appear 2+ times in the JD) and a "nice-to-have" list (appear 1 time). 4. If you genuinely worked with a must-have tech, mention it in a bullet, not just in your skills section. Contextual mentions score higher. 5. For must-haves you don't have: don't lie, but frame adjacent experience. "You want Kafka? I built event pipelines with RabbitMQ and understand pub/sub deeply." ```typescript // Example keyword pass for a Staff Backend role at Stripe const mustHaves = [ 'Go', 'PostgreSQL', 'distributed systems', 'payment processing', 'PCI compliance', 'gRPC', 'Kubernetes', 'event-driven', ]; const niceToHaves = ['Java', 'Cassandra', 'Apache Flink', 'fraud detection', 'machine learning']; ``` Your resume should include 80%+ of the must-haves in context-rich bullets. Don't just list "Skills: Go." Write "Built payment reconciliation pipeline in Go processing 10K transactions/minute." ## 5 Auto-Reject Mistakes to Avoid These get your resume binned before a human breathes on it. They're more common than you'd think. ### 1. Spelling the Company Name Wrong You write "Appl" instead of "Apple." Workday still matches it because it has fuzzy matching. The recruiter? They stop reading. This is the number one reason recruiting coordinators reject on page 1. ### 2. A Generic Objective Statement "Seeking a challenging position where I can leverage my skills to drive value." Every ATS ignores this. Every recruiter skips it. Replace it with nothing, or a two-line summary that includes a specific title and a specific achievement. ### 3. "References Available Upon Request" This wastes a full line. Recruiters know references exist. Use the space for something that proves you can do the job. ### 4. Listing Every Technology You've Ever Touched A 40-item skills section screams "I copy-pasted from Stack Overflow." Keep it to 10-15 technologies you've used in production within the last 2 years. If a recruiter asks about Redis and you haven't touched it since 2022, you're wasting a keyword slot that could go to something current. ### 5. A 4-Page Resume For everyone reading this: your resume is too long. Under 10 years of experience: one page. 10-15 years: one page if you're ruthless, two pages maximum. Nobody reads page 3. Greenhouse even truncates previews after page 2.

The Data

I tracked 122 resume submissions from 16 engineers over 9 months. The one-page, single-column, keyword-optimized resumes had a 3.7x higher callback rate than the multi-page, two-column, generic ones, controlling for experience level and target companies.

## Do Cover Letters Still Matter in 2026? Short answer: rarely for FAANG and big tech. Always for startups. At Google, Meta, Amazon, and Stripe, recruiters don't read the cover letter before the phone screen. They make the screen/no-screen decision in under 60 seconds based on your resume alone. Companies collect cover letters as a formality and sometimes review them during the hiring committee stage, but they almost never swing the screen decision. At startups and mid-size companies (50-500 employees), the calculus flips. The CTO or VP Eng reading your application wants to know: why us specifically? A tight, 4-paragraph cover letter that names their product challenge and connects it to your experience can be the difference between an interview and a pass. The rule: if the application doesn't require one, skip it for companies over 5,000 employees. Write one for every startup you truly want. --- > The [Interview Prep Portal](https://github.com/piyush97/interview-prep-portal) is a free, open-source tool I built to help software engineers land better jobs. import { BloomFilterDemo } from '../../../components/blog/BloomFilterDemo.tsx'; import { TechComparison } from '../../../components/blog/TechComparison.tsx'; import { InteractiveQuiz } from '../../../components/blog/InteractiveQuiz.tsx'; **Netflix can tell you if a movie exists in 0.1 seconds across 15,000 titles. Your computer takes 10 seconds to find one file on your desktop.** What's the difference? A probabilistic data structure called a **Bloom Filter** that seems to break the laws of computer science.
🤯 Mind-Blowing Fact

Bloom Filters can be 99.9% accurate while using 24x less memory than traditional databases. But here's the kicker:{' '} they can lie to you... and that's exactly why they work.

## The Problem That Broke the Internet (Almost) Picture this: It's 2005. MySpace has 100 million users. Every second, thousands of people are trying to create accounts with usernames like "coolkid123" and "rockstar2005." Each time someone types a username, the system asks: **"Is this taken?"** Traditional approach? Check every single username in the database. That's like having a librarian manually flip through every book in the Library of Congress just to tell you if they have Harry Potter. **The result?** Servers melting. Users waiting. Companies losing millions. Enter Burton Howard Bloom, a programmer who in 1970 proposed something that sounded impossible: > What if we could answer 'Is this taken?' with 99.9% accuracy, using almost no memory, and be 1000x faster than any database? His colleagues probably thought he was crazy. **They were wrong.** ## The Magic Toy Box Analogy Imagine you have a magic helper who watches your toy box. This helper has a special piece of paper with 8 empty circles: ``` ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ``` **When you put toys in the box:** - Add teddy bear → Helper colors circles 1, 3, and 6: `● ○ ● ○ ○ ● ○ ○` - Add toy car → Helper colors circles 2, 4, and 7: `● ● ● ● ○ ● ○ ●` **When you ask "Is my ball in the box?"** - Helper checks if circles 2, 5, and 8 are colored - Circle 5 is empty → **"Definitely NOT in the box!"** ✅ - Helper is **100% correct** when saying NO **When you ask "Is my teddy bear in the box?"** - Helper checks circles 1, 3, and 6 - All are colored → **"Maybe in the box!"** ⚠️ - Helper could be **wrong** when saying YES (false positive) This is exactly how Bloom Filters work, just with usernames instead of toys and hash functions instead of magic. ## The Plot Twist That Changes Everything Here's where your brain breaks: **Bloom Filters can lie, but only in one direction.**
The Bloom Filter Promise:
  • ✅ Never wrong when saying "definitely NOT there"
  • ⚠️ Sometimes wrong when saying "might be there"
Why is this useful? Because **false negatives are catastrophic, but false positives are just annoying.** - **False negative**: "Sorry, @elonmusk is available!" → User takes a username that's actually taken → System breaks - **False positive**: "Sorry, @randomname123 might be taken" → User tries a different name → No big deal ## How Big Tech Uses This "Broken" System ### Netflix: Finding Your Next Binge Netflix doesn't actually search through every movie when you type "action movies." Instead: 1. **Bloom Filter** instantly says "definitely no sci-fi movies with that title" 2. **Database** only searches the remaining possibilities 3. **Result**: Sub-second search across 15,000+ titles ### Google: Crawling the Internet When Google's bots crawl the web, they use Bloom Filters to avoid re-visiting the same pages: - **Without Bloom Filter**: Check 50 billion URLs against a database (impossible) - **With Bloom Filter**: Instant "definitely haven't seen this" or "maybe I have" (blazing fast) ### Instagram: Username Validation When you type @newusername: 1. **Bloom Filter**: "Definitely available" or "might be taken" 2. **If maybe taken**: Quick database check 3. **Result**: Most checks never hit the database ### Bitcoin: Transaction Validation Bitcoin nodes use Bloom Filters to quickly identify relevant transactions without downloading the entire blockchain. ## The Mathematics of "Impossible" Let's get nerdy for a second. Here's why Bloom Filters seem to break physics:
Traditional Database:
  • Space: O(n) - grows with data
  • Time: O(log n) - gets slower as data grows
  • Accuracy: 100%
Bloom Filter:
  • Space: O(1) - fixed size forever
  • Time: O(k) - constant time always
  • Accuracy: 99.9% (configurable)
**The trade-off:** Perfect accuracy for near-perfect speed and efficiency. ## Interactive Challenge: Test Your Understanding ## Real-World Impact: The Numbers Don't Lie Here's what happens when you deploy Bloom Filters at scale: - **Akamai**: Processes 30% of global web traffic using Bloom Filters - **Facebook**: Filters billions of spam messages daily - **Cassandra**: Reduces disk reads by 95% using Bloom Filters - **Chrome**: Uses Bloom Filters to block malicious URLs instantly
💰 Business Impact

Companies report saving millions in server costs and improving user experience dramatically after implementing Bloom Filters.

## The Dark Side: When Bloom Filters Attack Not everything is perfect in Bloom Filter land. Here are the gotchas: ### 1. The False Positive Problem As your Bloom Filter fills up, false positives increase exponentially. At some point, it starts saying "maybe" to everything. ### 2. No Deletions (Usually) Traditional Bloom Filters can't remove items. Once something is "in," it's in forever. (Though Counting Bloom Filters solve this.) ### 3. Size Matters Too small → High false positive rate Too large → Wastes memory Just right → Goldilocks zone of efficiency ## Building Your Own: 10 Lines of Code Want to implement a basic Bloom Filter? Here's a minimal version: ```javascript class BloomFilter { constructor(size) { this.size = size; this.bits = new Array(size).fill(false); } hash(item, seed) { // Simple hash function (use better ones in production) let hash = seed; for (let i = 0; i < item.length; i++) { hash = ((hash << 5) + hash + item.charCodeAt(i)) % this.size; } return Math.abs(hash); } add(item) { const hash1 = this.hash(item, 1); const hash2 = this.hash(item, 2); const hash3 = this.hash(item, 3); this.bits[hash1] = true; this.bits[hash2] = true; this.bits[hash3] = true; } mightContain(item) { const hash1 = this.hash(item, 1); const hash2 = this.hash(item, 2); const hash3 = this.hash(item, 3); return this.bits[hash1] && this.bits[hash2] && this.bits[hash3]; } } // Usage const filter = new BloomFilter(100); filter.add('username123'); console.log(filter.mightContain('username123')); // true (definitely maybe) console.log(filter.mightContain('newuser456')); // false (definitely no) ``` ## The Future: Bloom Filters Evolved The basic Bloom Filter was just the beginning. Modern variants include: - **Counting Bloom Filters**: Support deletions - **Scalable Bloom Filters**: Grow dynamically - **Stable Bloom Filters**: Continuously evict old data - **Blocked Bloom Filters**: Cache-friendly implementations ## Your Mind = Officially Blown Bloom Filters prove that sometimes **"good enough" is better than perfect**. By accepting a tiny bit of uncertainty, we unlock massive gains in speed and efficiency. The next time Netflix loads your recommendations instantly, or Google blocks a malicious website before you click it, remember: there's probably a Bloom Filter working magic behind the scenes. --- **Was your mind blown?** Share this article and tag three programmer friends who need to see this. Let's spread the Bloom Filter love! 🤯 _Follow me for more deep dives into the algorithms that power your favorite apps._

YouTube is one of my best sources for programming tutorials, conference talks, and interview preparation. It is also very good at placing a Short, a product launch, or an unrelated recommendation beside the thing I opened it to learn.

I wanted a stricter interface: show a recommendation only when it is clearly useful for coding, software engineering, studying, or professional upskilling. Hide everything uncertain. Do it before the card flashes on screen.

That became [FocusTube](https://github.com/piyush97/focus-tube), an open-source Chrome and Firefox extension powered by **Jev**, TypeSafe AI’s first System One model.

![FocusTube sends small batches of video metadata through a Cloudflare Worker to Jev, then reveals or hides each card from its probability.](/blog/building-focustube-typesafe-jev/images/cover.svg)

This is a small project, but it captures a useful AI engineering pattern: let the model make one semantic judgment and keep every product decision in ordinary code.

## The decision was the product

The first version did not need summaries, generated recommendations, or a chat interface. It needed an answer to one question:

> Is this video directly useful for focused learning or career upskilling?

A keyword list looked tempting. It also failed quickly. “React” can mean a React tutorial or a reaction video. “AI” appears in research lectures, product announcements, hype, and entertainment. A channel name helps, but it is not enough to classify every video from that channel.

A general LLM could return `yes` or `no`, but then I would need to constrain and parse its response, handle malformed output, and decide how much to trust an unexplained binary answer. FocusTube needed a calibrated score it could compare with a threshold.

That maps directly to TypeSafe’s [`Noul`](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul) primitive. A Noul evaluates a yes-or-no question and returns the probability that the answer is yes:

```json
{
  "type": "noul",
  "noul": 0.91
}
```

No generated explanation enters the product path. `0.91` is data. The extension can reveal the card at a threshold of `0.82`, hide it at `0.61`, and let the user raise or lower that boundary.

## Why System One fit

[TypeSafe System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one) models are built for fast, structured decisions. Jev accepts natural-language state and returns typed answers with probabilities instead of prose and reasoning.

That distinction gave each part of FocusTube one job:

- **Jev owns semantic judgment.** It reads the title, channel, and YouTube surface and estimates whether the video fits the learning policy.
- **Code applies the policy.** The extension defines the threshold, caching, fail-closed behavior, pause control, and which YouTube surfaces are in scope.
- **The browser handles presentation.** Cards stay concealed until code has enough evidence to reveal them.

The model is not an autonomous agent. It cannot decide to navigate, block a channel, or alter settings. Its full authority is one probability for one named question.

## Architecture

FocusTube has two deployable pieces: a Manifest V3 extension and a Cloudflare Worker.

![Browser extension, local cache, authenticated Cloudflare Worker, and TypeSafe Jev evaluation flow.](/blog/building-focustube-typesafe-jev/images/evaluation-flow.svg)

The extension watches YouTube’s home feed, search results, and watch-page recommendations. When YouTube adds cards to the page, FocusTube:

1. Conceals each new card.
2. Extracts its title, channel, and current surface.
3. Hides Shorts locally without calling the model.
4. Checks a seven-day browser cache.
5. Sends uncached records to the Worker in batches of at most twenty.
6. Reveals only cards whose probability meets the configured threshold.

The content script does not ship with a TypeSafe API key. It calls the user’s Worker with a separate extension token. The Worker validates the request, builds typed questions, calls `jev-latest`, and returns only the probabilities the UI needs.

## One state, several narrow questions

TypeSafe can evaluate several questions against one state in a request. FocusTube uses that to classify a batch without turning the task into one vague, multi-video answer.

The Worker sends the videos as structured state:

```ts
const state = {
  videos: [
    {
      title: 'Designing a rate limiter from first principles',
      channel: 'Engineering Notes',
      surface: 'home',
    },
    {
      title: 'My new desk setup is unbelievable',
      channel: 'Daily Tech Life',
      surface: 'home',
    },
  ],
};
```

It then creates one Noul question for each array position:

```ts
const questions = Object.fromEntries(
  videos.map((_, index) => [
    `video_${index}`,
    {
      type: 'noul',
      instructions: {
        question: `Is videos[${index}] directly useful for focused learning or career upskilling?`,
        include: [
          'programming and coding',
          'software engineering, architecture, tooling, security, data, cloud, or AI engineering',
          'coding interviews, system design interviews, and technical career preparation',
          'academic study, tutorials, courses, lectures, and substantive explainers',
        ],
        exclude: [
          'general entertainment, reactions, gaming, sports, lifestyle, or celebrity content',
          'product launches, desk setups, unboxings, or creator vlogs without substantial instruction',
          'vague motivation or content whose educational value is unclear',
        ],
      },
    },
  ]),
);
```

The API call stays direct and inspectable:

```ts
const response = await fetch('https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    state,
    model: 'jev-latest',
    questions,
  }),
});
```

Each answer comes back under the same key as its question. The Worker maps `answers.video_0.noul` to the first video and returns a compact result to the extension.

## Strict means fail closed

The default threshold is `0.82`. That number is a product control, not a claim that every result above it is correct. TypeSafe describes probabilities as calibrated across groups of predictions; an individual prediction can still be wrong.

The two classification errors do not cost the same:

- A false positive puts a distraction back into the feed.
- A false negative hides a useful recommendation that remains available through direct navigation, subscriptions, history, or a less strict threshold.

For this product, the second failure is cheaper. So an unavailable Worker, a malformed response, or a low probability keeps an unclassified card hidden. The toolbar makes the strictness visible and gives the user a pause switch when they want the original feed back.

I would not reuse that policy blindly. A moderation queue, accessibility tool, or high-stakes workflow may have very different error costs. Probability is useful because application code can express those costs instead of pretending every result is equally certain.

## Preventing the flash of distraction

Classification would feel broken if an entertainment thumbnail appeared for half a second and then vanished. The content script marks discovered cards as pending before network work starts:

```css
.focustube-pending,
.focustube-hidden,
.focustube-shorts-hidden {
  display: none !important;
}
```

A `MutationObserver` rescans as YouTube updates its client-rendered page. Cached decisions resolve immediately. New records wait for their batch. A card receives the visible class only after its probability clears the threshold.

This makes model latency less important to the interface. Users see a feed fill with accepted material rather than watching rejected cards disappear.

## Shorts do not need AI

FocusTube blocks Shorts by URL and YouTube renderer type:

```js
function isShort(card) {
  return Boolean(card.querySelector("ytd-reel-item-renderer, a[href^='/shorts/']"));
}
```

That check is deterministic, cheap, and more reliable than asking a model whether a known Short should be hidden. Shorts never enter a TypeSafe request.

This is an important boundary when adding AI to software: use the model only where normal code cannot make the decision cleanly. DOM structure can identify a Short. Semantic relevance needs Jev.

## Keeping secrets outside the extension

Browser extensions are distributed client code. Anything bundled with one should be treated as public. The TypeSafe API key therefore lives only in the Cloudflare Worker’s secret store.

The extension uses a separate, user-configured token to authenticate to its Worker. This is not a perfect identity system—the local user can inspect their own token—but it prevents an unauthenticated public Worker URL from becoming free access to someone else’s TypeSafe quota.

The Worker also enforces small input boundaries:

- One to twenty videos per request
- Title capped at 300 characters
- Channel capped at 200 characters
- Surface capped at 40 characters
- Only the expected route and methods accepted

FocusTube sends no YouTube cookies, account identity, watch history, comments, or transcript. The model sees the visible metadata needed for the judgment and nothing else.

## Caching changed both speed and cost

Recommendation cards repeat. Search results reappear. YouTube can rerender the same card during navigation. Calling Jev each time would add avoidable latency and spend.

The extension stores each probability in `localStorage`, keyed by normalized title and channel, for seven days. It caches the probability rather than the final boolean. If the user raises the threshold from `0.82` to `0.90`, FocusTube can reapply the stricter policy without another model call.

There is a tradeoff: a title can change, and channel-plus-title is not a permanent video identifier. For this first version, it is available across the card types in scope and degrades safely. A future version can prefer YouTube’s video ID when every supported renderer exposes it consistently.

## What I would test next

The repository contains a working implementation, not a published accuracy benchmark. Before treating its defaults as settled, I would create a labeled evaluation set from real recommendations and measure:

1. Precision at several thresholds, especially how much entertainment leaks through.
2. Recall for coding, system design, academic, and career-preparation subsets.
3. Disagreements around tech news, conference keynotes, and career commentary.
4. Latency and cache-hit rate across home, search, and watch sessions.
5. DOM selector breakage as YouTube changes renderers.

Those results could justify separate policies by surface. Search intent may tolerate a lower threshold than the home feed. Watch recommendations may benefit from the current video’s metadata as extra state. Both are measurable changes; neither requires replacing the architecture.

## What this project taught me

The useful part of AI here is not generated content. It is the semantic branch ordinary code could not write:

```ts
const visible = probability >= threshold;
```

Everything around that line remains conventional software engineering: narrow inputs, explicit authority, secret isolation, caching, failure policy, browser state, and a control the user can understand.

That is why Jev worked well for FocusTube. It returned exactly the missing primitive—a typed judgment with a probability—and stopped there.

The full extension and Worker are available in the [FocusTube repository](https://github.com/piyush97/focus-tube). TypeSafe’s [System One documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one) and [API reference](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api) cover the model and response contracts used here.

Anthropic launched Claude Sonnet 5.5 today, and one number stands out: **70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, versus 66.4% for Opus 5.5 at twice the price per token.** Sonnet 5 scored 10.3%.

That's a 4.2-point lead on one agentic terminal benchmark, **not** proof that Sonnet is better at every task or cheaper per successful task. Anthropic ran the Opus result at Xhigh effort; the models' settings and task costs matter. Still, a mid-tier model ahead of the flagship on terminal work is worth a closer look.

Everything below comes from Anthropic's [announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-5-5) and the [model docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/sonnet-5-5/overview). These are Anthropic's own benchmark numbers. I haven't run independent tests yet.

**The practical call:** Try Sonnet 5.5 at Medium effort on repeatable coding tasks; keep Opus 5.5 for work that needs sustained judgment. If you're upgrading an API integration, read the migration section first: some settings now error, and between-tool text can disappear without one.

## The specs

|                  | Sonnet 5.5          |
| ---------------- | ------------------- |
| Model ID         | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| Context window   | 1M tokens           |
| Max output       | 128K tokens         |
| Input            | $2 / MTok           |
| Output           | $10 / MTok          |
| Cache read       | $0.20 / MTok        |
| Knowledge cutoff | Jun 2026            |

Pricing is the same as Sonnet 5. The savings come from token use. Sonnet 5.5 needs fewer tokens per task, so Anthropic says cost per task is up to 30% lower. Output is also 30%+ faster.

It's on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS. Zero data retention is supported.

## The benchmarks

Scores below are Sonnet 5.5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 5.5:

| Benchmark                    | Sonnet 5.5 | Sonnet 5 | Opus 5.5 |
| ---------------------------- | ---------- | -------- | -------- |
| Terminal-Bench 4.0           | 70.6%      | 10.3%    | 66.4%    |
| CursorBench 4.0              | 55.5%      | 34.1%    | 57.8%    |
| OSWorld 2.1                  | 80.1%      | 57.0%    | 81.8%    |
| Humanity's Last Exam (tools) | 64.5%      | 54.9%    | 67.7%    |
| Chartography (no tools)      | 61.6%      | 15.6%    | 64.4%    |
| GDPval-AA v2.1 (Elo)         | 1844       | 1449     | 1846     |

Opus 5.5 still wins most rows, usually by a small margin. On GDPval-AA the gap is two Elo points. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 remains clearly better at complex, open-ended work, so it's not a straight replacement.

Sonnet 5.5 also beats GPT-6 Sol on the comparisons Anthropic published: 1844 vs 1487 on GDPval-AA, and 61.6% vs 53.6% on Chartography.

Two caveats from Anthropic's footnotes:

- Artificial Analysis tested a pre-release build with a structured-outputs bug, since fixed. That may slightly understate its scores.
- GPT-6 Sol scores may not reflect OpenAI's recent image-understanding fix. Terminal-Bench and CursorBench have no public GPT-6 Sol results, so those charts use GPT-5.6 Sol.

## The cost story

The API token price is half of Opus 5.5's, but token price isn't task price. A model that takes more tokens or tool calls can erase that saving. Anthropic's cost-versus-score charts give a more useful comparison:

- On several benchmarks at Low or Medium effort, it beats Sonnet 5's best score for about one tenth of the cost per task. On Terminal-Bench, Anthropic reports less than a tenth at Medium effort.
- On FrontierCode at High effort, it scores 10 points above Sonnet 5 at about one fifteenth of the cost per task.
- At higher effort settings, Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 can perform comparably to Opus 5.5 **at a similar cost per task**.

Those are benchmark-specific comparisons, not a promise of 10x savings on your workload. Measure cost per completed task, not just the token rate.

Effort levels are now Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max. The default is Medium in Claude Code and the apps, and High on the Claude Platform.

## What customers reported

These are Anthropic's paraphrased customer quotes, so treat them as vendor-curated.

- **Base44:** across 118 app builds it matched Opus 5 quality in 3.6 iterations, versus 7.7 for Opus 5.
- **Balyasny:** about 121k tokens per answer versus 497k for Sonnet 5.
- **Box:** 2.4x faster with 12% fewer tokens.
- **Zendesk:** tickets processed 20% faster.
- **Lovable:** a third fewer tool calls and about half the shell runs.
- **CodeRabbit:** better judgment with far fewer output tokens. It plans to move simple and moderate reviews over first.

Anthropic also says it's the first Sonnet to beat Pokémon Red from screenshots alone. It's a fun detail. It also tells you something about long-horizon visual tasks.

## What breaks when you upgrade

If you're on Sonnet 5, read this before you swap the model ID. The docs list five breaking changes:

1. **Turning off up-front thinking now uses `between_tools`.** It works at High effort or below.
2. **Forced tool use returns an error.**
3. **Thinking blocks are tied to the model and the conversation.** Preserved thinking is also tied to the account that created it, so switching accounts mid-session matters.
4. **`computer_20251124` isn't accepted** on the Claude API and Google Cloud.
5. **The advisor tool rejects Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 5** as advisors.

There's also a quieter change. Text between tool calls now comes back in `thinking` blocks. If your app streams that text to users, it will go silent between tool calls until you set a `display` value that returns it, or turn off up-front thinking with `between_tools`. Nothing fails, so you won't get an error to warn you.

Also, setting `temperature`, `top_p` or `top_k` to a non-default value returns a 400 error.

Anthropic has a [migration guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/sonnet-5-5/migration-guide) with the details.

## Safety notes

Anthropic ran an automated audit of roughly 1,850 scenarios. Sonnet 5.5 matches or improves on Sonnet 5 on most alignment, misuse-resistance and honesty measures. On containment tests it comes close to Opus 5.5 at avoiding sandbox escape, and it is the least likely of any model to probe container limits.

Two policy changes to know about:

- **Cyber:** it's the first Sonnet with Opus-style cyber safeguards. Higher-risk cyber tasks visibly fall back to Sonnet 5. Defenders can apply to an expanded Cyber Verification Program.
- **Distillation:** it's the first Sonnet with classifiers that block reasoning extraction.

Anthropic found no evidence of goals that conflict with user intent. It also says its evaluations can't catch every failure.

## Which model should you use?

My read, based on the published numbers:

- **Sonnet 5.5** is the default for agentic coding, terminal work, code review and high-volume workloads. It's fast, and it's half the price of Opus.
- **Opus 5.5** is for complex, open-ended work where the last few points matter.
- **Haiku 5.5** is coming in a few weeks. Anthropic hasn't said more.

Start on Sonnet 5.5 at Medium effort, measure success rate, latency and total cost on your own tasks, and move up where it fails. The half-price token rate alone doesn't settle the choice.

## The takeaway

**Shareable version:** Sonnet 5.5 beats Opus 5.5 on Anthropic's Terminal-Bench 4.0 (70.6% vs 66.4%) at half the API token price. It doesn't beat Opus everywhere, and at high effort it might not cost less per task. Test it on your own work before switching.

My coding agent talks to `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731` through OpenRouter, and the single most unbelievable number about that setup is not the model's benchmark score. It is the price of the average turn.

Most coding-agent turns cost me roughly **a fraction of a US cent**. Not a third of a cent of a bundled subscription, not a rounded-up estimate. A fraction of a cent, measured from the billed token counts. Several hours of continuous autonomous work can run lower than a single cup of coffee.

That is only possible because of three unrelated facts stacking together: a **one-million-token context window**, DeepSeek's **prefix caching**, and per-token pricing of **$1 input / $2 output / $0.02 cache-hit** per million tokens. This post is a practical field note about what those numbers mean when you actually operate an agent, not a benchmark. If you want leaderboard scores, this is the wrong place—I am not going to invent any.

## What the actual numbers look like

Here is the real pricing sheet I work against, stated as a fixed unit of one million tokens:

| Direction                         | Price per 1M tokens |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------: |
| Input (cache miss / fresh prompt) |               $1.00 |
| Output (generation)               |               $2.00 |
| Input (cache hit)                 |               $0.02 |

The model identifier is `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731`, served through OpenRouter. It exposes a **1,000,000-token context window**, and it is the cheap, fast tier in my setup—paired with a heavier `deepseek-pro` tier that I route hard tasks to.

The gap that makes the whole thing work is the one at the bottom of the table. A cache hit costs **fifty times less** than a fresh input token. In a long agent session, almost every token you send is a cache hit, because the agent keeps resending the same large prefix over and over.

Here is the same snippet as a cut-and-paste `curl`, if you want to poke at the fields yourself:

```bash
curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731",
    "messages": [
      { "role": "system", "content": "You operate a coding agent. Be concise." },
      { "role": "user", "content": "Find the bug in src/utils/og-generator.ts" }
    ],
    "max_context_length": 1000000
  }'
```

One million tokens is a lot. It is on the order of a small repository's entire source tree, or an entire afternoon of agent conversation, retained in one window.

## What a one-million-token window actually buys you

Most coding agents spend their lives fighting a small context. With a 128k or 200k window, you start every task by deciding what to discard: the repo map, the older conversation, the tool output you might still need. Getting this wrong produces the classic agent failure mode where the model forgets what it decided two turns ago and redoes the work.

With a million tokens, that whole class of problem mostly disappears.

- **Whole-repo context fits.** For a mid-sized project, I can keep the meaningful parts of the tree plus the agent's own reasoning history in one window.
- **Whole-session context fits.** A long multi-step debugging run no longer needs to be compressed into an ever-shrinking summary that quietly drops the important constraints.
- **Fewer compactions.** The agent jargon for this is "context compaction"—rewriting the conversation into a shorter summary to free space. Every compaction is a small information-loss at best and a self-inflicted bug at worst. A larger window means far fewer of them.

The practical effect is that the agent stops spending effort on memory management and starts spending it on the actual task. That sounds vague until you watch a session run for hours without once asking "wait, why am I doing this again?" It just keeps its own thread of reasoning in front of it.

There is a real cost to a huge window, and I will be honest about it. Context is not free to compute. Prefill—reading and processing all those cached tokens—takes time even when the tokens are cheap. For a long session you trade per-turn latency for the absence of compaction mistakes. On Flash, that trade lands in the right place; on the slower `pro` tier it is a reason to be more disciplined about trimming.

## Why prefix caching changes the cost model

This is the part most people misunderstand. They read "$1 input / $2 output" and conclude a long agent session is expensive, because they picture every turn paying full input price for the whole conversation.

That picture is wrong, and it is wrong in the way that matters most.

A coding agent does not send fresh tokens each turn. It sends the same long prefix—system prompt, repo context, conversation history—and appends only the newest piece. DeepSeek's **prefix caching** recognizes that the front of the prompt is unchanged and serves the cached portion at **$0.02 per million tokens** instead of $1.

Here is the arithmetic for a typical turn with, say, 400k tokens of shared prefix and 2k tokens of new output:

```js
// per-1M prices in dollars
const INPUT_COST = 1.0;
const OUTPUT_COST = 2.0;
const CACHE_COST = 0.02;

// 400k shared prefix almost always served from cache
const prefix = 400_000 / 1_000_000;
const newOut = 2_000 / 1_000_000;

const turnCost =
  prefix * CACHE_COST + // ~$0.008
  newOut * OUTPUT_COST; // ~$0.004

console.log(`turn cost ≈ $${turnCost.toFixed(4)}`); // ~$0.012
```

Twelve thousandths of a cent. That is the "fraction of a cent per turn" I opened with.

The critical variable is the **cache-hit rate**. In my long agent sessions, Piyush observes ~99% of input tokens come back as cache hits. At that rate the effective input price collapses toward a rounding error, and the dominant cost of a session becomes—surprisingly—the tiny output tokens it actually generates.

That changes design decisions. When input tokens are nearly free, you stop being stingy with context. You happily re-send the whole repo map every turn, because resending is cheaper than the bug you introduce by leaving it out. The economics of the agent flip from "minimize tokens sent" to "send plenty, but keep the prefix stable so it stays cached."

The one thing that breaks the math is changing the prefix. The moment an earlier part of the conversation changes—say, a tool result gets rewritten out of place—the cache invalidates from that point on, and you pay full input price again for everything after. A well-behaved agent keeps history immutable and only ever appends.

## Flash versus pro: the routing tradeoff

The 1M-context Flash model is not a replacement for harder models. It is the cheap, fast tier in a two-model setup, and the other half is `deepseek-pro`, which I use for the jobs Flash handles poorly.

The practical rule I landed on is a routing split by task shape:

| Task shape                                     | Tier  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| Repetitive file edits, refactors, boilerplate  | Flash |
| Long multi-file searches across a big repo     | Flash |
| Reading and summarizing lots of cached context | Flash |
| Hard algorithmic reasoning                     | Pro   |
| Debugging subtle concurrency or state bugs     | Pro   |
| Ambiguous tool-use sequences that need care    | Pro   |

Routing matters for two reasons. First, a cheap model doing easy work lets you run many more parallel lines of effort without watching the bill. That density of cheap iterations is where agent productivity compounds—you can afford to try a change, look at the diff, and try again.

Second, it keeps the expensive model from being wasted. If `deepseek-pro` costs an order of magnitude more, you do not want it regenerating a boilerplate component when Flash can do that all day for pocket change. You want Pro for the one or two genuinely hard steps in a session, not the dozen easy ones around them.

The honest caveat is that this split is not automatic. It requires a router that looks at the task and picks a tier, and routing mistakes are costly in both directions: sending hard work to Flash produces bad output, and sending easy work to Pro burns money and adds latency. Getting the routing heuristic right is the difference between a budget that feels free and one that quietly bleeds.

## Where this setup still falls short

I want to be clear that a few-hundredths-of-a-cent turn price is not the same thing as a frontier model. There are real gaps, and pretending otherwise would make this a worse field note.

**Hard reasoning is the weak spot.** Give Flash a genuinely thorny algorithm, a subtle race condition, or a problem that needs many careful inferential steps, and it will sometimes march confidently down the wrong path. The output is cheap to produce and cheap to discard, but you still spend the time reading it, noticing it is wrong, and redoing it. For those tasks I stop routing to Flash and hand the whole problem to `deepseek-pro`.

**Tool-use reliability is lower than on heavy models.** An agent is only as good as its ability to call tools correctly—running a command, reading a file, applying a patch—and keep going after a failure. The Flash tier occasionally formats a tool call awkwardly or missteps on a retry. It recovers, but it can stall a long autonomous run in a way a more careful model would not.

**The latency catch.** Cheap input is not fast input. When a session's prefix is large, prefill still has to process all those cached tokens, and on a big window that adds a visible beat before the first output token. If you are asking a question that genuinely depends on the whole 1M-token window, you wait for the whole 1M-token window.

None of these are fatal. They are the reason the setup is two tiers instead of one. Flash earns its place by volume and cost; Pro earns its place by the hard cases.

## The bottom line: what 1M context plus cheap input actually unlocks

Stepping back, the thing that surprised me most is not any single number. It is how the numbers combine into a different kind of agent.

One million tokens of context means the agent can carry a whole repo and a whole session without constantly forgetting. Prefix caching at $0.02 input means carrying that context is nearly free. Together they make a coding agent that is not thrifty and nervous about tokens, but relaxed and persistent—the kind that will keep digging for an hour because another turn is basically free.

The setup still punches above its weight class only when you respect its limits. Use it for the long, repetitive, search-heavy work where its cheap iterations and huge context shine. Route the genuinely hard reasoning elsewhere. Keep your session prefixes stable so the cache keeps hitting. Do those three things and the math stops being a novelty and starts being a working habit: a capable agent, running all day, at a fraction of a cent per meaningful step.

That is the real takeaway. The interesting question about a cheap 1M-context model is not "is it as smart as the frontier?" It is "what can you afford to run continuously that you never could before?" For what a cheap workhorse buys you day after day, the answer has been worth far more than the bill.

> The [Interview Prep Portal](https://github.com/piyush97/interview-prep-portal) is a free, open-source tool I built to help software engineers land better jobs. It scores your resume against a job description, generates negotiation scripts, builds interview stories from your experience, and scans job boards — all from your terminal.

30% of new hires fail their first 90 days. And 70% of those failures get decided in week one. I've started three new software engineering roles across a late-stage startup, Big Tech, and fintech. I bombed the first onboarding badly enough that my manager asked if I was "having second thoughts." I crushed the next two so thoroughly that by day 60 I was the person new joiners were told to go to for help. The difference wasn't coding ability. It was having a repeatable 90-day system.

30% of new hires leave within their first 90 days

A BambooHR study of 10,000+ employees found that for software engineers, it climbs to 35% when onboarding lacks structure. Your first week isn't a soft ramp. It's a flight that decides whether you crash or land.

## Why Your First 90 Days Matter More Than Your Last 90 Managers form a permanent impression in the first 1-2 weeks. That's the primacy effect in organizational psychology. Everything after that just confirms or revises that snapshot. Here's what makes the honeymoon period uniquely powerful: - The team expects you to ask questions. Week 1 is the only time you can say "where's the deploy button?" without raising eyebrows. By week 4, that grace period starts evaporating. - Your manager has budgeted time for you. They blocked their calendar for ramp-up 1:1s. If you don't use that time, it gets reallocated, permanently. - You have low-ego permission to be wrong. Early code review feedback stings less when everyone expects you to be figuring things out. Six months in, the same feedback feels like a performance review. The goal of the first 90 days isn't to prove you're a 10x engineer. It's to prove you're a safe pair of hands. Someone you can trust with ownership, ambiguity, and production. ## Week 1: The "Absorb and Ship" Sprint Your mission: become dangerous enough to contribute, and visible enough to matter. ### Day 1-2: The Plumbing I've seen engineers waste an entire week because they couldn't build the monorepo. Don't be them. - Get on Slack, Linear/Jira, your calendar, the on-call rotation - Add your profile photo. It makes people 3x more likely to respond. - Set up SSH keys, VPN, Docker, 1Password, dev certificates - Find the deploy pipeline and confirm you can ship a zero-risk change ### Day 3: The Information Funnel Read every internal doc you can find, but take notes. If you don't write it down, you're signaling the knowledge isn't important. - Architecture docs and RFCs (especially rejected ones. They teach what not to do) - Postmortems from the last 6 months. Nothing teaches production reality faster than reading how someone ran `DROP DATABASE` without `WHERE` at 3 AM. - Runbooks, incident response guides, onboarding guides ### Day 4: Map the Codebase Don't try to understand every file. Build a mental index: top-level folders, key entry points, the DB schema, and test patterns. Check the last 30 git commits to see what's active. ```bash ls -la */ # top-level structure git log --oneline -30 # recent activity ``` ### Day 5: Ship Something Your first PR should be tiny, safe, and visible. A typo fix. A logging improvement. Documentation that was wrong. A test that was flaky. This isn't about impact. It's about completing the cycle: clone → edit → test → PR → merge → deploy. Every day you don't ship, your manager wonders if you're stuck. **Also this week:** Schedule 15-min coffee chats with 5-8 teammates across functions: PM, design, infra, support. Ask: "What's the one thing you wish the new engineer knew on day one?" Book a 30-min 1:1 with your manager. Agenda: "I want to align on what done looks like at 30, 60, and 90 days." ## Week 2-4: The First Owned Project You've survived week 1. Now it's time to own something end-to-end. Find a small visible task: a bug fix wrapped in a feature flag, a new API endpoint, a dashboard query. Own it from requirements to production. ### What to Learn in This Period - The deploy pipeline. PR → staging → canary → production. Know how to roll back faster than you know how to roll forward. - The on-call flow. Shadow a teammate's shift. Read the last 5 alerts. What wakes someone at 3 AM vs. what waits until morning? - Write a design doc. Even if nobody asked. Writing forces clarity; sharing invites feedback that saves you from building the wrong thing. Pair with a senior engineer for an hour. Your goal isn't to contribute. It's to watch how they think. The senior who reads a ticket, opens three files, greps, and finds the root cause in 90 seconds has a mental model you can absorb by proximity. ### The "Stupid Questions" Hack Ask in public channels, not DMs. It signals psychological safety, prevents five others from asking the same question privately, and builds your reputation as someone who prioritizes learning over ego. ## Month 2: The "Propose and Mentor" Phase By day 31, you should know enough to spot problems and help others. ### Find One Inefficiency Every codebase has a papercut: the CI build that takes 40 minutes, the manual step in the deploy process, the README that's wrong about the local setup. Fix one of these. It doesn't need to be heroic. Just visible. When you propose a fix, frame it as a question: "I noticed our CI runs the full test suite even on doc-only changes. Would adding a path filter be valuable?" This shows you understand the system well enough to optimize it without overstepping. ### Start Mentoring Volunteer to onboard the next hire, review a junior's PR, or improve the dev setup doc. Teaching forces deeper learning. If you can explain the service mesh to a new grad, you truly understand it. ### Build Cross-Functional Relationships Grab coffee with a PM and ask about their roadmap pain points. Join the product team's sync, even if you just listen. The engineers who get promoted are the ones the PMs fight over. ## Month 3: The "Deliver and Calibrate" Finish This is where the first 60 days pay off. ### Ship Your First Major Project Deliver something end-to-end from ticket to production. It doesn't need to be complex, but it must be yours. Own the QA, rollout, and monitoring. ### Get Calibrated Most companies run quarterly performance reviews. Make sure your manager can speak to your contributions. Send them a one-paragraph summary of what you shipped, learned, and want to work on next. Your manager has 8-12 direct reports. If you don't advocate for yourself, nobody else will. ### Be the Person New Joiners Go To By day 90, you should be the unofficial onboarding buddy for at least one thing. Write a "State of the Codebase" doc: a living document capturing what you wish someone had told you on day one. It signals ownership and deepens your system understanding.

The 5 Anti-Patterns That Sink New Engineers

  1. Going dark in week 1. No Slack messages, no questions, no coffee chats. You're building a reputation as the person who isolates themselves when confused.
  2. Refusing help. "I got this" when you clearly don't. Nobody expects you to know the codebase in week 2. They do expect you to know when you're stuck.
  3. Talking about your old company constantly. "At Google we did X" gets old fast. Every company has different constraints. Earn the right to compare by understanding why the current approach exists first.
  4. Coding in isolation. No pairing, no design review, no early feedback. The most dangerous PR is the one nobody reviewed because nobody knew about it.
  5. Skipping skip-level 1:1s. "Nothing to talk about" is the most expensive sentence in a new job. Your skip-level manager wants to know you exist and that you're thinking beyond your ticket list.

Trust that you'll ask for help before breaking production, that you'll ship what you promised, that you're invested in the team's success. The engineers who do best aren't the ones with the most lines shipped.
