Your spreadsheet wants GPT-6.1 Sol. Your production incident wants proof. OpenAI's [GPT-6.1 Sol announcement](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-sol/) makes a compelling pitch: near-Astra intelligence for coding, computer use, and professional work at one-fifth of Astra's standard API input and output token prices. The important word is **near**. That is OpenAI's positioning, not a guarantee that Sol will match Astra on your repository or your agent's tasks. For developers, the interesting question is whether the quality difference is small enough to justify the price difference. The [Sol model documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6.1-sol) explicitly recommends comparing the two on your own work. ## What the prices actually say At standard API rates, the [published Sol prices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6.1-sol) and [Astra prices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra) are: - **Input, per million tokens:** Sol $2; Astra $10. - **Cached input, per million tokens:** Sol $0.10; Astra $1. - **Output, per million tokens:** Sol $10; Astra $50. The one-fifth comparison applies to **uncached input and output**, not every line item. Cached input is one-tenth Astra's listed rate. Sol also lists cache writes at $2.50 per million tokens, versus $12.50 for Astra. For a request with 100,000 uncached input tokens and 20,000 output tokens, those rates imply about **$0.40 on Sol versus $2 on Astra**, before any tool fees. That is a pricing illustration, not a measured workload or a prediction of how many tokens either model will need to finish the same job. Both model pages say prompts above 272,000 input tokens incur higher rates for the **full request**: twice the input and cache rates, and 1.5 times the output rate. A million-token context window does not mean a million tokens at the base price. ## A large context window, with practical limits Sol's documented context window is **1,050,000 tokens**, with a maximum of **922,000 input tokens** and **128,000 output tokens**. It accepts text and images and produces text; audio and video are not supported input or output modalities. Its documented knowledge cutoff is April 30, 2026. That capacity is useful for a codebase, a long document set, or a multi-step agent trace, but capacity alone says nothing about whether a particular answer will be accurate. Long prompts also increase both cost and the chance that important evidence gets buried. Test with the inputs you actually intend to send, including the large-context pricing threshold. ## The API details that change implementation The model ID is `gpt-6.1-sol`. Its `reasoning.effort` values are `low`, `medium` (the default), `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`; `none` and `minimal` are not supported. The docs direct developers to the **Responses API for tool calling**. Chat Completions is supported **without tool calling**. Under Responses, the documented tool list includes web search, file search, code interpreter, hosted shell, computer use, and MCP. The model also supports structured outputs, streaming, function calling, and prompt caching. Fine-tuning and predicted outputs are not supported. If your application depends on a specific tool or endpoint, check the [model's support tables](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6.1-sol) rather than assuming that every capability carries over from Astra. Sol supports US and EU data residency, but the docs say Fast mode is unavailable with EU data residency. Tool calls can carry separate fees, and Fast, Batch, Flex, and regional processing have different prices. Those details matter when calculating the cost of an actual agent run rather than a bare text request. ## Should you switch? ![Original two-panel meme: the spreadsheet says “Ship it. Cheaper!” while the test suite asks to see the evals](/blog/gpt-6-1-sol/images/eval-meme.svg) Treat Sol as a candidate for workloads where Astra's quality is valuable but its price limits how often you can use it: coding tasks, computer-use flows, and document-heavy professional work. Do not treat “near-Astra” as an independent benchmark result. Run the same representative tasks through both models, at the reasoning effort you plan to ship, and compare successful outcomes, human corrections, latency, and **total** cost including retries and tools.
Quick gut check before switching models
  1. Pick ten real tasks, including failures and long prompts.
  2. Run both models with the same tools and reasoning effort.
  3. Compare completed tasks and human corrections before comparing the bill.
If Sol clears your quality bar, the listed token prices leave meaningful room to scale. If a small failure rate creates expensive rework, Astra may still be the cheaper choice for that particular workflow. The launch headline gets Sol onto the shortlist; your evaluation should decide where it belongs.

I closed the lid, drove to a coffee shop, and the agent that had been refactoring a two-hundred-file monorepo for ninety minutes was still running when I opened it back up. The terminal was sitting in the same pane, the same scrollback, the same place in the diff. The only thing that had changed was the Wi-Fi network.

The thing that had been quietly killing me was not the answer the agent eventually produced. It was the ninety minutes it had been working while I was not, and the five minutes I would have spent restarting it every time the laptop slept. Coding agents are good now. They run for hours. They refactor whole trees, they run test suites, they wait on pull-request reviews. The bottleneck, again, was not the model. It was the terminal.

[Herdr](https://herdr.dev/) is the runtime that makes this routine. It is a single Rust binary that holds your coding agents' terminals open across laptop closes, network drops, and machine restarts — and tells you, without you to clicking, which one is stuck. After a few weeks it has changed how I think about agent work entirely.

> **The short version:** Herdr is one Rust binary that keeps your coding agents' terminals alive when the laptop sleeps, the SSH drops, and the Wi-Fi changes — and twenty agents show up the moment you install it.

## Why every agent session is a borrowed process

Here is the part that was wearing me down. A coding agent runs in a terminal. A terminal belongs to a TTY. A TTY dies when the SSH session drops, when the lid closes, when the laptop sleeps, when the Wi-Fi flips to a captive portal, when the user's shell exits because they closed their emulator. Every "session" for an agent is a borrowed process. The agent is a tenant in someone else's house, and the landlord can evict it any time.

The hidden cost of that eviction is not the lost compute. It is the lost context. The agent had read the diff, planned the refactor, hit the first migration, decided to keep the old behavior for the second one, and was halfway through the third. The eviction kills the reasoning, not the work — and the model has to start the reasoning over.

I do not want a desktop Electron app to manage my agents. I do not want a hosted SaaS IDE. I want the terminal to keep being the terminal, and I want the agents to keep being the agents, and I want neither of them to be at the mercy of my lid. The author of Herdr described the same trap in the [announcement post about joining Y Combinator](https://herdr.dev/blog/herdr-is-joining-y-combinator/): the bottleneck on his own agents was himself.

## What Herdr actually is

Herdr is one Rust binary. No Electron, no daemon that ships its own GUI, no installer that pulls a kernel module. It runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows from the same binary, and it owns the terminals your agents live in.

The architecture is the part that matters. From the [Herdr concepts doc](https://herdr.dev/docs/concepts/):

> "By default, Herdr runs as a background server plus one or more attached clients. The server owns panes and process state. The client is the terminal UI attached to that server. Detach the client with `ctrl+b q`. The server and agents continue running."

Read that twice. The server is the runtime. The client is just a view onto it. You can attach a client from your laptop, walk away, close the laptop, open it on a different network, and `herdr` again. The server is still there. The agents are still there. The pane layout comes back exactly as you left it.

The README headlines it: **"the runtime your coding agents live on"** ([github.com/herdrdev/herdr](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr)). The marketing subhead on the site captures it tighter: _Run them anywhere. Leave them running._

## Install in sixty seconds

```bash
curl -fsSL https://herdr.dev/install.sh | sh
```

That is the whole pitch on Linux and macOS. Homebrew also has it: `brew install herdr`. Nix users can pin a version with `nix profile install github:herdrdev/herdr/v0.x.y`. Windows has a PowerShell variant. All of these are documented at [herdr.dev/docs/install](https://herdr.dev/docs/install/).

After install, `herdr` launches or attaches to the default background session. From the [quick start doc](https://herdr.dev/docs/quick-start/): "You do not manage sockets. If you detach, agents keep running."

## The runtime mental model

The Herdr author gave the cleanest version of the model in the [YC announcement post](https://herdr.dev/blog/herdr-is-joining-y-combinator/):

> "A terminal pane belongs to an agent. A pane belongs to a tab. Tabs belong to a project."

Four nested objects, four operators moves. They are not abstractions; they are the things you actually split, name, and attach to.

| Concept       | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | How you make one                                                              |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Workspace** | The top-level project container. One workspace per repo, task, or investigation. The sidebar rolls up agent state from inside it so you can see which project needs attention. ([concepts](https://herdr.dev/docs/concepts/)) | `herdr workspace create --cwd ~/project --label api`                          |
| **Tab**       | A layout inside a workspace. Use tabs to separate views like `agents`, `logs`, `server`, or `review`. Addressable from the CLI and the socket API.                                                                            | `herdr tab create --label logs`                                               |
| **Pane**      | A real terminal. Splittable, addressable as `w<n>:p<n>`. Renders output, sends input back, and survives client detach.                                                                                                        | `herdr pane split w1:p1 --direction right`                                    |
| **Agent**     | A process Herdr recognizes inside a pane. Twenty detected kinds out of the box — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode, Grok, the rest. ([agents](https://herdr.dev/docs/agents/))                                             | `herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane "$review_pane" -- -m gpt-5.4` |

If you have used tmux or zellij, the verbs will feel familiar. The keyboard prefix is `ctrl+b`, and the bindings out of the box are:

| Action               | Key                     |
| -------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Split right          | `prefix+v`              |
| Split down           | `prefix+minus`          |
| New tab              | `prefix+c`              |
| Next / previous tab  | `prefix+n` / `prefix+p` |
| Workspace navigation | `prefix+w`              |
| New workspace        | `prefix+shift+n`        |
| Detach client        | `prefix+q`              |

If you have not, the [quick start](https://herdr.dev/docs/quick-start/) is mouse-first; you do not have to learn the prefix to get going.

## Never hunt for the stuck one

This was the second thing that wore me down, and it is the one Herdr fixes most directly. From the [homepage](https://herdr.dev/):

> "Herdr reads every pane and marks each agent working, blocked or idle. When one stops and needs an answer it says so, so you don't go pane by pane looking for whoever is waiting on you."

The five states, per the [concepts doc](https://herdr.dev/docs/concepts/):

- `blocked` — needs input or approval
- `working` — actively running
- `done` — finished, unseen
- `idle` — finished, seen
- `unknown` — Herdr cannot classify it

For most agents the state comes from lifecycle hooks or session identity. For a few it comes from a screen-manifest match on the bottom of the buffer. For a custom agent that Herdr does not recognize, the CLI inside the pane can publish its own state — see the section below on custom integrations.

You can read state without scripting:

```bash
herdr agent get w1:p2                       # snapshot one pane
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked   # wait until the agent genuinely needs you
```

That `wait` primitive is the one I now use most. It blocks until another agent is in a state worth your attention, instead of firing keystrokes into a pane and hoping. From the [agent automation docs](https://herdr.dev/docs/agent-automation/): "A script can control them, or one agent can create work for other agents, inspect their state, and collect their results."

## The always-running story

Let me retell the lid-closed story as the technical story, because that is what Herdr actually buys you. From the [homepage](https://herdr.dev/):

> "Herdr isn't an app you keep open. It's a server running in the background, and the terminals live inside it. Close the lid or drop the network and the agents keep working; restart the machine and Herdr brings the layout back and resumes their sessions."

Three concrete operator paths, all documented at [herdr.dev/docs/how-to-work](https://herdr.dev/docs/how-to-work/):

1. **Local.** `herdr` launches and attaches to the default session. `prefix+q` detaches the client. The server and every agent keep running.
2. **Plain SSH, tmux-style.** Run Herdr on a remote box, attach from your laptop over SSH. The remote server owns the panes; the local client just renders.
3. **Thin client.** `herdr --remote workbox` — or `herdr --remote ssh://you@server:2222` — attaches to a server elsewhere and renders the panes locally. Reattach from any device with a keyboard.

There is even a `Work from your phone` subsection in that doc, paired with SSH clients like moshi. I have not used it in anger, but the fact it is documented is the point: the runtime has stopped caring where you are.

## The runtime is also an automation layer

This is the section that turned Herdr from a multiplexer I was trying into a multiplexer I keep. The CLI surface is the same surface agents drive, which means a script — or another agent — can drive it.

```bash
# Workspace + tab + pane
herdr workspace create --cwd ~/project --label api
herdr tab create --label logs
herdr pane split w1:p1 --direction right --ratio 0.333
herdr pane run w1:p2 "npm test"
herdr pane read w1:p2 --source recent --lines 50

# Agent primitives (the headline CLI surface)
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane "$review_pane" -- -m gpt-5.4
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff" --wait --timeout 120000
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
herdr pane wait-output w1:p3 --regex "passed|failed" --timeout 120000
```

That is a working reviewer loop. Start an agent in a pane, prompt it, wait until it is blocked, read its recent output, branch on what it says. A second agent can be scripted to do the same in another pane.

For agents Herdr does not natively recognize, every pane ships with a runtime contract: `HERDR_ENV`, `HERDR_PANE_ID`, `HERDR_BIN_PATH`, `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH`. A pane can publish its own lifecycle state:

```bash
"$HERDR_BIN_PATH" pane report-agent "$HERDR_PANE_ID" \
  --source custom:my-agent --agent my-agent --state working
```

That is enough to wire your home-grown agent into Herdr's state sidebar, the wait primitive, and the socket API. The full contract is at [herdr.dev/docs/integrations](https://herdr.dev/docs/integrations/).

If you want to talk to the runtime as data, not as a process:

```bash
herdr api snapshot                           # live session.snapshot as JSON
herdr api schema --output herdr-api.schema.json  # pin the socket protocol
```

Both are documented at [herdr.dev/docs/socket-api](https://herdr.dev/docs/socket-api/). Treat the runtime like a database.

## When NOT to use it

I would not trust this post if it did not say so.

1. **You do not run coding agents.** Herdr is opinionated for terminal-resident agent workflows. If you are happy in VS Code + Copilot and your agent never runs longer than a coffee, the runtime is overkill. A `tmux` session is fine.
2. **You need a host with the agent GUI, not the terminal.** Herdr does not render Claude Code's TUI prettier; it keeps the real TUI alive. If you want a managed IDE experience, Herdr is the wrong shape.
3. **You want plug-and-play agent coordination across machines.** Herdr runs everywhere and persists across machines, but cross-machine orchestration is not the v0.8.x story. Use the runtime for durability, not for fleet coordination.
4. **You are on Windows ARM64.** Windows ARM64 runs the x86_64 build under emulation; functional but not native. ([herdr.dev/docs/install](https://herdr.dev/docs/install/))

For everything else — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode, Grok, the rest — Herdr is what makes the agent workflow survivable. From the [homepage](https://herdr.dev/): "Runs what you already run. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode, Grok and the rest. Herdr doesn't wrap them or replace them, it just owns their terminals."

## The Herdr cheat sheet

Pin this. Drop it in your shell rc. Add the aliases that match how you actually work.

```text
# 1. Install (Linux / macOS)
curl -fsSL https://herdr.dev/install.sh | sh

# 2. Lifecycle
herdr                 # launch / attach to the default background session
prefix + q            # detach the client (server + agents keep running)
herdr server stop     # end the session

# 3. The runtime hierarchy
herdr workspace create --cwd ~/project --label api
herdr tab create --label logs
herdr pane split w1:p1 --direction right --ratio 0.333
herdr pane run w1:p2 "npm test"

# 4. Agent scripting
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane "$review_pane" -- -m gpt-5.4
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff" --wait --timeout 120000
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000

# 5. Remote attach
herdr --remote workbox
herdr --remote ssh://you@server:2222

# 6. Debug / inspect
herdr api snapshot
herdr agent explain reviewer
```

And if you want it shorter, aliases:

```bash
alias h='herdr'
alias hs='herdr server stop'
alias ha='herdr --remote'
alias hap='herdr agent prompt'
alias haw='herdr agent wait'
alias hws='herdr workspace create --cwd "$(pwd)" --label'
```

## Get the runtime, then keep going

[Herdr](https://herdr.dev/) is Y Combinator-backed, open source, and at v0.8.2 as of this week. It is one Rust binary. It does not replace your terminal, your editor, or your agents; it owns the place they all live so they survive everything you do to your laptop.

If you want one CLI that keeps your coding agents alive across the lid closes you are going to keep doing, install it before lunch. If you want to read more first, the [concepts doc](https://herdr.dev/docs/concepts/) is the right next stop — five minutes, and you will know what every verb in this post means.

If this changed how you think about agent runtimes, the next post will change how you think about something else.

And if Herdr ends up earning its place on your machine, [star the repo](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr) so the maintainers know their bet on a one-binary runtime landed.

There's a catch: as of today you can't download it. You can call it through Moonshot's API and apps, and Moonshot [says](https://www.kimi.ai/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro) the full weights will be released **by Nov 4, 2026**. Until they are, "open weight" is a promise.

This post covers what changed, which numbers someone other than Moonshot has checked, and what to test before you switch an agent over.

## What is Kimi K3.1 Pro? Same model, more post-training

K3.1 Pro uses the same architecture as K3. Moonshot calls it "a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute," trained with joint RL across "hundreds of downstream domains."

The specs carry over from K3, which I covered in [Kimi K3 Is Open Weight, but You Still Need a Datacenter to Run It](/blog/kimi-k3-open-weights-datacenter):

- **2.8T total parameters, ~104B active** per token (MoE)
- **1,048,576-token** context window
- Text and image input

So the hardware story hasn't changed. When the weights land, you'll still need a multi-accelerator cluster to run them, not a workstation. What changed is how well the model behaves once it's running.

## Kimi K3.1 Pro benchmarks vs Claude Opus 5.5, sorted by who measured them

Most launch coverage mixes vendor claims and independent results into one table. I've kept them apart.

### Independent: Artificial Analysis

| Metric                            | Kimi K3 | Kimi K3.1 Pro                         |
| --------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Intelligence Index                | 44      | **55** (4th overall)                  |
| Terminal-Bench 4.0                | 13%     | **67%** (highest of any model tested) |
| GDPval-AA (Elo)                   | 1,534   | **1,846** (3rd)                       |
| AutomationBench-AA                | 58%     | **73%**                               |
| AA-Omniscience hallucination rate | 53%     | **44%**                               |
| Humanity's Last Exam              | 47%     | **52%**                               |

The three models ahead of it on the Index are Claude Opus 5.5 (58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (56), and Muse Wonder Full (56). On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it scored above Sonnet 5.5 (64%).

Terminal-Bench is the number I'd weight most heavily. Moonshot claimed 65.7% in its own Claude Code harness, and AA measured 67%. A vendor coding claim held up under someone else's harness on launch day, and that doesn't happen often.

### Vendor-reported: Moonshot

These come from [Moonshot's tech blog](https://www.kimi.ai/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro) and haven't been independently reproduced:

- **Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon:** 61.2 vs 55.95 for K3. Moonshot owns both the benchmark and the harness.
- **BenchCAD with tools:** 92.7, behind Opus 5.5 (96.2) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9), level with Claude Fable 5.1 (92.6).
- **Internal finance evals:** Business Operation went from 8.9 to 37, Research from 58.8 to 70.4.
- **Kimi Hallu Bench Hard:** claim-level hallucination fell from 23.4% to 8.3%.

### Two hallucination numbers that measure different things

Moonshot reports **8.3%** and AA reports **44%**. Both can be true because they measure different things.

- Moonshot's 8.3% counts false claims inside responses, with tools available.
- AA's 44% counts how often the model answers wrong when it should have said it didn't know.

Both moved in the right direction. The 44% is the one to remember if your agent answers questions without retrieval. In close to half of those cases it still guesses instead of abstaining.

## Kimi K3.1 Pro pricing: cheaper per token, flat per task

Per 1M tokens, [confirmed by Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/kimi-k3-1-pro-launch-benchmarks):

|                   | Input     | Cache hit | Output     |
| ----------------- | --------- | --------- | ---------- |
| Kimi K3           | $3.00     | $0.30     | $15.00     |
| **Kimi K3.1 Pro** | **$2.00** | **$0.20** | **$10.00** |

There's no long-context surcharge, so the price is the same at token 1,000 and token 1,000,000. One million input tokens plus 200K output costs **$4.00** on K3.1 Pro versus **$6.00** on K3.

Per task the saving is smaller. AA measured 55K output tokens per Index task, up 14% from K3, and a cost of **$1.98 per task**, which it calls roughly equal to K3. The model is cheaper per token but spends more tokens thinking, so measure your own workload before you budget for a 33% drop.

`kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed` is the same model served 2 to 3 times faster. [OrcaRouter lists it](https://www.orcarouter.ai/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro-release) at $4 input and $20 output, double the standard rate.

## How to use the Kimi K3.1 Pro API

The API is OpenAI-compatible. From the [quickstart](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-1-pro-quickstart):

```bash
curl https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MOONSHOT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "kimi-k3.1-pro",
    "reasoning_effort": "high",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain this stack trace"}]
  }'
```

Four things will break a drop-in swap from another model:

1. **You can't turn reasoning off.** `reasoning_effort` accepts `low`, `high`, or `max`, and **defaults to `max`**. If latency spikes after you switch, check this setting first.
2. **Sampling is fixed.** `temperature=1.0`, `top_p=0.95`, `n=1`, and both penalties at 0 are locked. Leave them out of your requests. OrcaRouter reports that other values return an error.
3. **Return the full assistant message.** In multi-turn and tool-calling loops, send back the complete assistant message, not just `content`. Streaming returns `reasoning_content` and `content` as separate deltas.
4. **You need to top up first.** The model unlocks after at least $1 in credit, and your cumulative top-up sets your rate-limit tier.

## Moonshot removed some of its hacking ability on purpose

This is the most unusual part of the release.

Moonshot filtered cyberattack-related material out of the training data before the open release. The reason it gave, as [reported by TNW](https://thenextweb.com/news/moonshot-kimi-k3-1-pro-open-weight-cyber), is to avoid pushing the frontier of freely available offensive capability. On Moonshot's in-house exploit benchmark:

| Model                          | Real-vuln exploit score |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| K3.1 Pro, before the filtering | 90.5%                   |
| DeepSeek V4.1-Flash            | 85.7%                   |
| **K3.1 Pro, as released**      | **81.0%**               |
| Kimi K3                        | 33.3%                   |

Even after the filtering, it scores far higher than K3. Moonshot reduced the capability but didn't remove it. Weights can also be fine-tuned once they're public, so treat 81% as the starting point, not a ceiling.

For defenders: if you run open models in security tooling, K3.1 Pro will be very capable and will still be somewhat restricted. Test it on your actual use cases. Don't assume either way.

## What we still don't know

- **Whether the weights ship on time.** Nov 4 is a promise, and AA's "leading open-weights model" label depends on it.
- **The license.** Moonshot's blog doesn't state one. K3's license terms may or may not carry over.
- **Third-party serving.** Real price and speed competition starts when providers other than Moonshot can host the model. That can't happen before the weights are out.
- **Independent checks of the finance and CAD numbers.** So far they're vendor-only.
- **Behavior across a full 1M-token context.** It's supported. Whether quality holds at that length is a separate question that no published evaluation has answered yet.

## Should you switch to Kimi K3.1 Pro?

- **Coding-agent builders on Opus or Sonnet:** run your own eval. The independent Terminal-Bench result says it's worth an afternoon. Set `reasoning_effort` explicitly and track cost per task, not per token.
- **Teams on Kimi K3:** switch. It's the same architecture, it's cheaper per token, and it scores 11 Index points higher. Strip your sampling parameters first.
- **Teams waiting to self-host:** wait for the Nov 4 weights and the license, then plan hardware using the same numbers as K3.
- **Anyone answering factual questions without retrieval:** the 44% abstention failure rate is better than before, but it's still high. Keep retrieval in the loop.

When K3 came out, the open-weight story was mostly about access. With K3.1 Pro, an open-weight model is close enough to the top proprietary models that the choice now depends on cost, latency, and hosting control. Run your own benchmarks to find out which matters for you.

## Kimi K3.1 Pro FAQ

### When will the Kimi K3.1 Pro weights be released?

Moonshot says the full weights will be released by November 4, 2026. Until then, the model is only available through Moonshot's API and Kimi apps.

### How much does Kimi K3.1 Pro cost?

$2.00 per 1M input tokens, $0.20 per 1M cached input tokens, and $10.00 per 1M output tokens, with no long-context surcharge. That's a third cheaper than Kimi K3.

### Is Kimi K3.1 Pro better than Claude Opus 5.5?

Overall, no. Opus 5.5 scores 58 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, and K3.1 Pro scores 55. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Artificial Analysis measured K3.1 Pro at 67%, the highest of any model it tested.

### What is the Kimi K3.1 Pro API model ID?

`kimi-k3.1-pro`, or `kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed` for the faster variant. The API is OpenAI-compatible at `https://api.moonshot.ai/v1`.

### Can I run Kimi K3.1 Pro locally?

Not on a laptop or a single GPU. It has 2.8T total parameters, the same as Kimi K3, so self-hosting it will take a multi-accelerator cluster once the weights are out.

> **Update, October 23, 2026:** Moonshot has released a post-trained successor. See [Kimi K3.1 Pro: benchmarks, pricing, API and open weights](/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro-open-weight-gap). Moonshot AI just put one of the largest AI model checkpoints ever released on Hugging Face. You can download it without asking for API access, waiting for an enterprise contract, or trusting that a model provider will keep the same endpoint alive next year. There is only one small problem: **the download is 1.56 terabytes**. That number is not an estimate from a launch slide. I counted the 96 `.safetensors` weight shards in the [official Hugging Face repository](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3) and summed their published file sizes: **1,560,936,091,448 bytes**. On a connection sustaining a full 1 Gbps, the weights alone would take about three and a half hours to transfer. At 100 Mbps, the theoretical minimum is almost 35 hours. Storing the files is the easy part. Kimi K3 has **2.8 trillion total parameters**, activates **104 billion parameters for each token**, supports a **1,048,576-token context window**, and uses native visual input. Moonshot's own deployment guidance recommends a supernode with **64 or more accelerators**. So yes, Kimi K3 is open weight. No, it is not a laptop model. That apparent contradiction is the most important part of this release. Kimi K3 does not put frontier intelligence on every desk. It changes who is allowed to operate it, preserve it, modify it, study it, and sell access to it. The gatekeeper moves from **permission** to **compute**.

The Kimi K3 paradox

The weights are open enough to download, restricted enough to have a revenue clause, and large enough that most developers will still rent access from somebody else.

This is not a hands-on model review. Launch-day API comparisons would be misleading without the same harness, reasoning budget, tool environment, and repeated runs. This is an evidence audit of what Moonshot released on July 27, 2026, what the architecture means, what the license permits, what independent evaluation has established, and why weights that almost nobody can run locally still matter. ## Kimi K3 at a glance | Property | Kimi K3 | | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | | Architecture | Mixture of Experts (MoE) | | Total parameters | 2.8 trillion | | Activated parameters | 104 billion per token | | Layers | 93 | | Routed experts | 896 | | Experts selected per token | 16, plus 2 shared experts | | Attention layers | 69 Kimi Delta Attention + 24 Gated MLA | | Context window | 1,048,576 tokens | | Vision encoder | MoonViT-V2, 401 million parameters | | Weight format | MXFP4 weights, MXFP8 activations | | Published checkpoint | 96 shards, approximately 1.56 TB | | Recommended inference engines | vLLM, SGLang, TokenSpeed | | Official deployment guidance | Supernodes with 64 or more accelerators | | License | Custom Kimi K3 License | Sources: the [Kimi K3 model card](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3), [technical report](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/Kimi-K3/blob/main/k3_tech_report.pdf), and [technical blog](https://www.kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3). ## What Moonshot actually released The headline is the full model checkpoint, but the release is larger than a directory full of tensors. Moonshot published: - the [Kimi K3 weights and model card](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3); - a detailed [technical report](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/Kimi-K3/blob/main/k3_tech_report.pdf); - a custom [Kimi K3 license](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3/blob/main/LICENSE); - recipes for serving the model with [vLLM](https://recipes.vllm.ai/moonshotai/Kimi-K3), [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Moonshotai/Kimi-K3), and [TokenSpeed](https://lightseek.org/tokenspeed/recipes/models#kimi-k3); - [FlashKDA](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/FlashKDA), MIT-licensed CUDA kernels for Kimi Delta Attention; - [MoonEP](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/MoonEP), an MIT-licensed expert-parallel communication library; and - [AgentENV](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/AgentENV), an MIT-licensed distributed system for running and resuming agent sandboxes at scale. That surrounding infrastructure matters. A model architecture is useful only if somebody can execute it efficiently. Kimi Delta Attention needs specialized kernels. A sparse model with hundreds of experts needs a way to route tokens across accelerators without one overloaded expert slowing every other device. Long-running coding agents need environments that can pause, resume, fork, and retain filesystem state. The release therefore exposes three different layers: ```text Model intelligence Kimi K3 weights and technical report Inference machinery FlashKDA + vLLM/SGLang/TokenSpeed support Agent infrastructure MoonEP communication + AgentENV sandboxes ``` The weights receive the headlines. The infrastructure determines whether the weights become a usable ecosystem rather than a 1.56 TB museum exhibit. There are still important things Moonshot did **not** release. The complete pre-training dataset is not available. The report describes training methods, reinforcement-learning environments, and infrastructure, but it is not a fully reproducible recipe that lets another lab recreate K3 from raw data. Open weights give outsiders the trained artifact; they do not expose every decision that produced it. ## How can a 2.8-trillion-parameter model use only 104 billion parameters? Kimi K3 is a **Mixture of Experts**, or MoE, model. The simplest way to understand MoE is to separate the model's total knowledge capacity from the amount of machinery used for one token. A conventional dense model uses essentially the same parameter blocks for every token. An MoE model contains many specialized feed-forward blocks called experts. A router scores those experts and sends each token through only a small subset. K3 has 896 routed experts. It selects 16 for each token, with two additional shared experts. The routed fraction is only about **1.8% of the expert pool** at a time. ```text Incoming token │ ▼ ┌──────────────┐ │ MoE router │ scores 896 routed experts └──────┬───────┘ │ selects 16 ▼ ┌────┬────┬────┬─────────┬────┐ │ E7 │ E42│ E91│ ... │E811│ + 2 shared experts └────┴────┴────┴─────────┴────┘ │ ▼ Combined representation → next layer ``` This is why both of these statements can be true: 1. Kimi K3 contains 2.8 trillion parameters. 2. It activates 104 billion—about **3.7% of the total**—for a token. The benefit is sparse computation. K3 can increase total model capacity without paying the arithmetic cost of a dense 2.8T model on every token. But sparse computation is not sparse ownership. The router can choose different experts for the next token, request, or user. All expert weights must remain available somewhere in the serving system. You cannot keep only today's 16 experts and delete the remaining 880; the next token may need a different combination. A restaurant analogy helps, as long as we do not stretch it too far. One meal may use only 16 specialists, but the restaurant still needs the full kitchen because the next order can require another team. MoE reduces how many cooks touch one plate. It does not shrink the building. ### Three architectural ideas behind K3 MoE is only one part of the design. The report organizes K3 around information flow across sequence length, network depth, and model width. **1. Kimi Delta Attention across sequence length.** KDA is a recurrent, linear-attention mechanism intended to process long sequences more efficiently than applying full quadratic attention at every layer. K3 interleaves three KDA layers with one Gated Multi-head Latent Attention layer. The periodic global-attention layers retain unrestricted token-to-token interaction. **2. Attention Residuals across depth.** A conventional residual stream repeatedly accumulates each layer's output. Attention Residuals let a layer selectively retrieve representations from earlier blocks instead of accepting the entire history with equal weight. Think of it as giving depth its own retrieval mechanism. **3. Stable LatentMoE across width.** K3 scales to 896 routed experts while trying to keep routing and training stable. MoonEP addresses a related systems problem: if too many tokens select experts on one accelerator, that device becomes the bottleneck. Its dynamic redundant-expert design aims to keep the work balanced across ranks. Moonshot says these changes, together with its training and data recipes, deliver roughly **2.5 times better scaling efficiency than Kimi K2**. That wording matters. It is a company-reported scaling-law result about capability gained per training compute. It does **not** mean K3 is automatically 2.5 times faster or cheaper to serve. ## Why a sparse model still weighs 1.56 TB K3 uses quantization-aware training with **MXFP4 weights** and **MXFP8 activations**. Four-bit weights are a major reason a 2.8T-parameter checkpoint can fit into roughly 1.56 TB rather than several terabytes more. Yet four bits multiplied by 2.8 trillion parameters is already about 1.4 TB before accounting for scales, metadata, non-weight files, and format overhead. Compression makes the release possible. It does not make it small. The runtime also needs more than static weight storage: - memory for active computations; - recurrent and attention state; - buffers for expert routing and cross-device communication; - image representations for multimodal requests; - cache or state for long conversations; - and capacity for concurrent users. The advertised one-million-token context window makes the systems problem harder. Maximum context is not free memory, instant prefill, or perfect recall. A provider must ingest the prompt, maintain the model's state, schedule work, and decide what can be cached. Long agent sessions also branch, call tools, retry failed actions, and append large tool outputs. Moonshot's [official blog](https://www.kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3) recommends deploying K3 on supernode configurations with **64 or more accelerators** because inference benefits from a large high-bandwidth communication domain. That is a recommendation, not a formally published minimum. Creative operators will try slower storage offloading, unusual quantizations, fewer devices, and expert streaming. The trade-off will be latency, throughput, context capacity, or all three. The early [r/LocalLLaMA launch thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1v8364f/kimi_k3_weights_now_released/) captured the problem perfectly. The most popular joke was: **"How do I download RAM in Hugging Face?"** Underneath the joke were serious debates about multi-node B200/B300 systems, storage capacity, tokens per second, and whether self-hosting could ever beat paying an inference provider. Those comments are useful signals, not benchmark data. Hardware prices and throughput estimates posted during launch-day excitement should not be repeated as facts without measured deployments. The reliable conclusion is narrower: **K3 is datacenter-class software today.** ## Downloadable, local, and open source are three different claims AI discussions often compress three separate ideas into one word: _open_. | Question | What it means | Kimi K3 | | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | | Can I download the trained parameters? | Open weights | Yes | | Can a typical developer run it privately on local hardware? | Local accessibility | No, not realistically at full scale today | | Can I reproduce, modify, and redistribute the complete system under a standard open-source license? | Open-source reproducibility | Not fully | Moonshot repeatedly calls K3 an open-source model in its product documentation. The more precise description is **open weight with a custom license**. The [Kimi K3 License](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3/blob/main/LICENSE) grants broad rights to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, sell, deploy, and fine-tune the software and weights. It then adds commercial conditions that standard permissive licenses such as MIT or Apache 2.0 do not contain. The two conditions most businesses need to notice are: 1. If a company operates a model-as-a-service business and it or its affiliates exceed **$20 million in aggregate revenue over any consecutive 12 months**, it must reach a separate agreement with Moonshot before using K3 commercially. 2. If a commercial product using K3 exceeds **100 million monthly active users** or **$20 million in monthly revenue**, the product must prominently display "Kimi K3" in its interface. Internal use and access through Moonshot's official products or certified partners receive exceptions described in the license. This does not make the release meaningless. Most individual developers, researchers, startups, and internal enterprise deployments gain broad rights. But "anyone can download it" is not the same as "anyone can use it for any purpose without additional conditions." The distinction matters because licensing determines who can build a competing API business—the exact group best equipped to operate a 1.56 TB model. The release opens the weights while preserving leverage over large commercial serving companies. A concise description is: > Kimi K3 is openly downloadable, commercially conditional at scale, and operationally inaccessible to ordinary local hardware. That is less exciting than "frontier AI is now open source," but it is more accurate. ## Does Kimi K3 actually compete with proprietary frontier models? Moonshot's strongest claim is not model size. It is that an open-weight model now operates near the proprietary frontier across coding, reasoning, visual work, and long-running agents. The company's own technical report is unusually direct about the limit: K3 **still trails Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol overall**. Its position changes by benchmark. | Benchmark | Kimi K3 | Claude Fable 5 | GPT-5.6 Sol | What the table suggests | | ------------------ | ------: | -------------: | ----------: | ------------------------ | | DeepSWE | 67.5 | 70.0 | 73.0 | K3 trails both | | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | 88.3 | 88.0 | 88.8 | Near parity | | ProgramBench | 77.8 | 76.8 | 77.6 | K3 narrowly leads | | FrontierSWE | 81.2 | 86.6 | 71.3 | Between the two | | SWE-Marathon | 42.0 | 35.0 | 39.0 | K3 leads this evaluation | These are reported results, not a controlled experiment proving one model is universally better. The [benchmark footnotes](https://www.kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3) reveal why: - K3 often uses the Kimi Code harness; - other models may use Claude Code, Codex, Terminus, or whichever harness produced their best result; - all K3 results use maximum reasoning effort; - some Fable 5 runs may include fallback behavior; - some GPT-5.6 Sol runs may encounter cyber guards; - several comparisons cite external leaderboards while others were run by Moonshot; - and Kimi Code Bench is an internal benchmark. A coding agent is the combination of a model, prompt, tools, context manager, sandbox, retry policy, and token budget. Change the harness and you change the system being measured. Comparing models under different harnesses may reflect the product a user can actually access, but it does not isolate raw model quality. The honest launch-day conclusion is therefore: - K3 has credible evidence of frontier-adjacent performance; - it wins some reported evaluations and loses others; - Moonshot's own report does not claim it is best overall; - and independent same-harness replication is still needed. ### An independent check from UK AISI and CAISI The most useful independent evidence available at launch comes from the [UK AI Security Institute and the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/preliminary-assessment-of-kimi-k3s-cyber-capabilities). Their preliminary evaluation examined offensive cyber capabilities before the weight release. The result was mixed: - K3 scored **32% on ExploitBench**, above GLM-5.2 at 24%; - it achieved arbitrary code execution on **0 of 41** ExploitBench samples, while the most capable closed models averaged 20 of 41; - on a 32-step simulated corporate-network attack, K3 reached step 17 on average, compared with 11 for GLM-5.2 and 28.5 for the leading closed models; - it completed the full simulated attack in 1 of 10 attempts; - and its safeguards did not prevent it from attempting offensive cyber operations in the evaluation. This does not settle K3's general capability. The assessment was preliminary and covered a selective set of cyber tasks. It does provide something the launch benchmarks cannot: an evaluator other than Moonshot finding the same broad pattern—**K3 advances the open-weight frontier, but a measurable gap remains on difficult tasks.** It also raises a security question familiar from [MCP and tool-calling agents](/blog/ai-agents-mcp-security-crisis): once capable weights are downloadable, provider-side safeguards are no longer a durable control boundary. Defenders gain a model they can inspect and run privately. Attackers gain the same permanence and configurability. ## Why do the weights matter if you cannot run them at home? This is where the release becomes more than a record-setting file transfer. ### 1. Inference providers can compete with the creator A closed model has one official seller. The provider controls price, regions, rate limits, retention policies, safety behavior, and deprecation. Open weights allow independent operators to compete on: - price per token; - latency and geographic location; - privacy and data residency; - context limits; - quantization; - fine-tuning; - tool-use policies; and - service reliability. Most developers may still call an API, but they no longer have to call **one specific API**. Moonshot's official service launched at **$0.30 per million cache-hit input tokens, $3 per million cache-miss input tokens, and $15 per million output tokens**. Those prices are a snapshot, not a permanent property of the model. Once more providers deploy K3, the market can test how much of that price reflects compute, utilization, software quality, or margin. ### 2. Enterprises can keep control of sensitive workloads A bank, hospital, government agency, or large software company may care more about control than local affordability. Running K3 inside an approved environment can offer: - data that does not leave the organization's infrastructure; - fixed model versions for auditability; - predictable retention policies; - custom security controls; - and freedom from unilateral API deprecation. That does not mean self-hosting is automatically cheaper. Accelerators are only the beginning. A production deployment needs networking, cooling, power, observability, failure recovery, model engineers, and enough demand to keep expensive hardware utilized. Idle GPUs can make a theoretically cheap token extremely expensive. The [Hacker News technical-report discussion](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49070985) centered on exactly this trade-off. Commenters proposed aggressive cost estimates for large racks, while others pointed out staffing, colocation, liquid cooling, concurrency, and idle capacity. Both sides can be right for different utilization curves. ### 3. Researchers can inspect a stable artifact An API is an experience. Weights are an artifact. With the checkpoint, researchers can study activations, routing behavior, quantization, long-context failure, safety tuning, model editing, and fine-tuning. They can test the same revision months later. They can preserve it even if Moonshot changes the hosted product. That permanence is easy to underestimate. Closed providers can silently update system prompts, safety filters, routing, context management, or the underlying model while keeping the same product name. A downloaded checkpoint can be hashed, archived, and evaluated repeatedly. ### 4. K3 can become a parent, not just a product The full model may be too large for consumers, but it can generate training data, supervise smaller models, and support distillation or specialist fine-tuning. The most important downstream result may be a smaller model that does not exist on launch day. Open-weight ecosystems often compound this way: ```text Large released checkpoint ↓ Independent evaluation and serving work ↓ Quantizations, fine-tunes, distillations, adapters ↓ Smaller and more specialized deployable models ``` K3's 1.56 TB size is therefore both a limitation and a source asset. The original model is difficult to operate. Its outputs, architecture, and learned representations can still seed systems that are easier to deploy. ### 5. Capability cannot be withdrawn A downloadable model cannot be fully recalled because a vendor changes strategy, a product fails, or a regulator pressures one endpoint. Access can become difficult; repositories can disappear; licenses can be disputed. But once the files are widely copied, the capability persists. That persistence is valuable for scientific reproducibility and operational continuity. It is also why releasing capable weights creates a different security profile from exposing the same model through a monitored API. ## The real shift is from model monopoly to infrastructure competition K3 does not eliminate centralization. It changes where centralization happens. With a proprietary model, control concentrates at the model lab. With a 1.56 TB open-weight model, control can spread across multiple hosting companies and large enterprises—but it still concentrates around organizations that own accelerators, high-bandwidth networking, power, and inference expertise. ```text Closed model User → one model vendor → one policy and price surface Kimi K3 weights User → competing inference providers → same base weights, different services └──────────→ private enterprise clusters └──────────→ research and downstream models ``` The bottleneck moves through the stack: | Closed-model bottleneck | Open-weight K3 bottleneck | | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | | Permission to access the model | Ability to obtain enough compute | | One provider's price | Provider competition and utilization | | One safety and policy layer | Operator-specific controls | | Vendor-controlled model lifecycle | Infrastructure and maintenance burden | | Limited inspection | Deep access, but incomplete training provenance | This is still a meaningful redistribution of power. A market with ten K3 providers is structurally different from a market with one K3 endpoint, even if an individual developer rents tokens in both cases. The lesson is not that open weights failed because the model does not fit on a gaming PC. "Local AI" and "competitive model markets" are different goals. K3 advances the second far more than the first. For engineers designing large AI products, this turns model routing into an architectural choice rather than a permanent vendor marriage. The capability-aware routing ideas in my [million-user AI chat system design](/blog/ai-chat-system-design-million-users) become more practical when several operators can serve the same base model under different latency, privacy, and price profiles. ## What we still do not know Launch day is the worst time to confuse available numbers with settled truth. Several questions need real deployments and independent evaluation. ### Real serving performance We need end-to-end tokens per second, time to first token, prefill latency, and cost under realistic agent workloads. A single-user decode benchmark does not tell us how K3 behaves with concurrent long-context sessions, tool outputs, retries, and branching trajectories. ### Minimum viable hardware Moonshot recommends 64 or more accelerators, but operators will test smaller clusters, offloading, lower-throughput configurations, and future quantizations. "Can boot" and "can serve economically" are different standards. ### One-million-token quality We need tests of retrieval, reasoning, instruction retention, and contradiction handling across the full window. The official report warns that generation can become unstable if a harness fails to preserve K3's complete thinking history or switches models mid-session. A context-window number measures accepted input length. It does not measure how well every part of that input influences the answer. ### Same-harness model comparisons The launch table mixes harnesses and evaluation sources. Strong conclusions require repeated tests with the same prompts, tools, sandbox, context policy, reasoning budget, and correctness criteria. ### Router behavior after post-training An MoE system lives or dies by routing. Independent operators need to understand expert-load distribution, specialization, hot experts, communication overhead, and whether post-training creates pathological imbalance on real traffic. ### License interpretation The custom thresholds are readable; their application to affiliates, derivative models, unusual service structures, and cross-border businesses may still require legal analysis. Downloadability does not remove license risk. ### Security after unrestricted adaptation The UK AISI/CAISI evaluation tested a hosted pre-release system. Open weights let operators alter prompts, post-training, scaffolding, budgets, and safeguards. Defensive and offensive capability may look different once independent teams optimize the complete system. These unknowns are not reasons to ignore the release. They are reasons to resist turning a model card into a verdict. ## Who should care right now? **Individual developers:** use a hosted K3 service if its quality, privacy terms, and price fit your work. Do not buy hardware for the full model based on launch-day estimates. **Local-LLM enthusiasts:** watch for expert streaming, quantizations, distillations, and smaller derivatives. The full checkpoint is more useful as an ecosystem parent than a workstation target. **Enterprises:** compare total cost of ownership, not GPU cost alone. Include concurrency, utilization, staffing, networking, cooling, failure recovery, licensing, and the value of data control. **Researchers:** the weights, report, and supporting infrastructure create a rare opportunity to study a near-frontier MoE system beyond an API boundary. **AI product teams:** treat open weights as leverage. A portable model option can improve negotiating power and reduce dependency even when a third party still hosts the inference. ## Open weights did not remove the gate. They moved it. Kimi K3 is not the best model on every benchmark. It is not reproducible from an entirely open training pipeline. Its custom license is not unrestricted. It will not run usefully on a normal developer workstation. Moonshot says as much about the performance gap, while the repository and license make the other limitations visible. And yet the release matters. A 2.8-trillion-parameter, native multimodal, long-context model with credible frontier-adjacent coding and agent capability can now be downloaded, archived, inspected, modified, independently hosted, and used to train what comes next. No single API provider has exclusive technical custody of that artifact. The phrase "democratizing AI" is too imprecise for what happened. K3 did not make frontier inference equally affordable. It widened the set of institutions that can own and operate the capability, and it gave researchers and downstream builders raw material they did not have before. **Kimi K3 did not put a frontier model on every desk. It put one outside the walls of a single AI lab—and made compute, rather than permission, the next gatekeeper.** --- ## Sources and methodology Research current as of **July 27, 2026**. Repository sizes, download counts, prices, integrations, and independent evaluations will change. ### Primary sources - [Kimi K3 official technical blog](https://www.kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3) - [Kimi K3 model card and weights](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3) - [Kimi K3 technical report](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/Kimi-K3/blob/main/k3_tech_report.pdf) - [Kimi K3 License](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3/blob/main/LICENSE) - [Kimi K3 API guide](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-quickstart) - [FlashKDA](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/FlashKDA) - [MoonEP](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/MoonEP) - [AgentENV](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/AgentENV) ### Independent and community sources - [UK AISI/CAISI preliminary assessment of Kimi K3's cyber capabilities](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/preliminary-assessment-of-kimi-k3s-cyber-capabilities) - [Hacker News discussion of the technical report](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49070985) - [r/LocalLLaMA launch discussion](https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1v8364f/kimi_k3_weights_now_released/) - [Quartz launch coverage](https://qz.com/moonshot-ai-kimi-k3-open-weights-download-072726) The checkpoint size was calculated from Hugging Face's repository API by summing the published sizes of all 96 `.safetensors` files. A model that can write a function is not necessarily a model that can repair a repository. The latter has to find the right file, avoid unrelated edits, run the right test, and stop when it has enough evidence. That is the interesting question behind [JetBrains' October 8 release of Mellum2.1](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/10/mellum2-1-gets-to-work-a-fast-open-model-for-coding-agents/), a 12B-total-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 2.5B active parameters, released under Apache 2.0. JetBrains says the architecture stayed the same as Mellum2; most of the change was post-training, including reinforcement learning in repositories with shell and file-editing tools.

On its [model card](https://huggingface.co/JetBrains/Mellum2.1-12B-A2.5B-Thinking), JetBrains reports **47.0% on SWE-bench Verified** for Mellum2.1 Thinking, versus **2.0% for Mellum2 Thinking**, using its own evaluation pipeline. That is a striking _vendor-reported_ difference, not a prediction that 47% of your issues will be fixed. The card specifies a shared Pi v0.73.1 harness with shell/file tools, 114K context, up to 16K tokens per turn, and each model's default sampling. Change the harness, task mix, or time budget and the comparison changes too.

The useful takeaway isn't “switch models.” It's **test the entire worker, not just the model**. A local agent may be an excellent cheap first pass for a narrow, well-tested job; it might be the wrong choice for a migration spanning five services.

## A small repo trial, not a leaderboard victory lap

Pick **five closed issues** whose fixes already have tests. Hide the solution commits from the candidate's workspace, but retain them for grading. Include at least one issue requiring navigation across files and one where the first plausible fix is wrong. Run every candidate from the same base commit in an isolated worktree or disposable container, with the same tool permissions and time/token budget. No network or production credentials unless the task truly requires them.

For each run, record:

1. **Outcome:** did the original failing test pass, and did the full relevant suite remain green? A passing suite alone can miss an incomplete fix; compare behavior against the issue's acceptance criteria.
2. **Scope:** how many files changed outside the expected area? Inspect the diff, including test deletions and config changes.
3. **Intervention:** did a human have to redirect the agent, repair its patch, or select a different tool?
4. **Cost and latency:** measure wall time, tokens if exposed, and peak memory for the _whole agent run_. “2.5B active” is not a hardware-memory specification: the model has 12B total parameters, plus runtime overhead and KV cache.
5. **Reproducibility:** repeat a couple of tasks with another seed or run. One lucky patch isn't a reliable routing policy.

Keep a holdout issue outside the tuning set. If you change the prompt or harness after looking at a failure, rerun that holdout before trusting the improvement. Never compare two models with different file access and then attribute the result solely to weights.

## A routing decision you can practice

You have a local worker with read/write access to a disposable worktree. Which task gets an _automated candidate patch_ first? Open a case, make your call, then read the tradeoff.

<details>
<summary>Case A: A utility function fails on empty input; the regression test already exists</summary>

**Good first candidate.** Give the agent the failing test and a bounded file scope. Accept only a patch that passes that test and the surrounding suite; review the diff. Small blast radius, cheap oracle.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Case B: Rotate production signing keys across three services with no integration tests</summary>

**Do not auto-route.** The absence of a reliable oracle and the credential blast radius dominate model speed. First design the rollout and rollback with a human owner, then delegate isolated implementation pieces in a credential-free sandbox.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Case C: A flaky integration test passes locally but fails in CI</summary>

**Investigate first.** Ask the worker to collect hypotheses and evidence without changing files. A green local run isn't evidence that the CI race is fixed. Reproduce the failure under the relevant CI conditions before accepting a patch.

</details>

This isn't a vendor-specific flow. You can run the same trial against a hosted model or a different local worker. The point is to set the task boundary and acceptance test _before_ seeing a persuasive answer.

## Serving details that change the experiment

The [Mellum2.1 Thinking card](https://huggingface.co/JetBrains/Mellum2.1-12B-A2.5B-Thinking) documents vLLM serving with `--reasoning-parser qwen3`, and adds `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser hermes` when using tools. Those flags matter for an agent evaluation: a chat endpoint that answers coding questions but cannot emit parseable tool calls is testing a different workflow. The card lists a 131,072-token context length; it does **not** mean every local machine can serve that maximum efficiently. Choose a context limit your hardware can actually sustain and record it with the results.

JetBrains also [describes](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/10/mellum2-1-gets-to-work-a-fast-open-model-for-coding-agents/) both a Thinking model for longer tasks and an Instruct variant for shorter responses. Don't silently mix them in a comparison. Pin the model revision, serving stack, prompt, harness version, permissions, and budget. Then run the same repo issues again when any of those change.

If the trial shows good patches on narrow tasks, use the local worker as a **proposer**: it writes a branch, deterministic checks run, and a person reviews before merge. If it fails the test, keep the failure trace. That is useful data for choosing a narrower task or a stronger fallback, not a reason to loosen the release gate.

In the evolving landscape of self-hosted infrastructure, the tools we choose can dramatically impact our efficiency, security, and peace of mind. After years of loyal service from Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM), I recently made the leap to SWAG (Secure Web Application Gateway) by LinuxServer.io—and the results have been nothing short of transformative.

This isn't just a story about swapping one reverse proxy for another; it's about embracing a more comprehensive, flexible, and powerful approach to managing web applications in a homelab environment.

## Why Consider a Migration?

Before diving into the migration process, let's address the fundamental question: **Why change something that works?**

Nginx Proxy Manager has been a beloved solution in the self-hosting community for good reasons:

- 🖥️ **User-friendly web interface** that simplifies SSL certificate management
- 🚀 **Easy setup** with Docker Compose
- 🔒 **Let's Encrypt integration** for automated certificate renewal
- 🧩 **Proxy host management** through an intuitive dashboard

However, as my self-hosted infrastructure grew more complex, I began encountering limitations that prompted me to explore alternatives.

## Enter SWAG: More Than Just a Reverse Proxy

SWAG by LinuxServer.io isn't simply a reverse proxy—it's a comprehensive web application gateway that combines:

- 🌐 **Nginx** (the powerful web server)
- 🔐 **Certbot** (for Let's Encrypt SSL certificates)
- 🔍 **Fail2Ban** (for intrusion prevention)
- 🛡️ **GeoIP2** (for location-based restrictions)
- 📊 **PHP** (for web applications)
- 📈 **Reverse proxy configurations** (for various applications)

![SWAG Components Architecture](/blog/migrating-nginx-proxy-manager-to-swag/images/architecture.svg)

This all-in-one approach eliminates the need for multiple containers while providing significantly more flexibility and control.

## The Migration Journey: Challenges and Solutions

### 1. Understanding the Configuration Paradigm Shift

The first challenge was mental: Nginx Proxy Manager abstracts much of the Nginx configuration through its UI, while SWAG embraces configuration files directly.

**NPM Approach:**

```
Configure everything through web UI → Black box magic → Working proxy
```

**SWAG Approach:**

```
Edit nginx config files → Restart container → Working proxy with complete control
```

This shift from GUI-driven to file-driven configuration initially seemed daunting but ultimately provided the flexibility I was seeking.

### 2. Planning the Migration Strategy

I opted for a parallel deployment strategy:

1. Set up SWAG alongside my existing NPM installation
2. Configure one service at a time in SWAG
3. Test thoroughly before switching DNS
4. Gradually migrate all services
5. Decommission NPM once everything was verified

This approach minimized downtime and allowed for easy rollback if needed.

### 3. Setting Up SWAG with Docker Compose

My initial SWAG configuration looked something like this:

```yaml
version: '3'
services:
  swag:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/swag:latest
    container_name: swag
    cap_add:
      - NET_ADMIN
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=1000
      - TZ=America/New_York
      - URL=yourdomain.com
      - SUBDOMAINS=wildcard
      - VALIDATION=dns
      - DNSPLUGIN=cloudflare
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config
    ports:
      - 443:443
      - 80:80
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - proxy
```

After launching SWAG, I was immediately impressed by the organized directory structure in the `/config` volume:

```
/config
├── nginx
│   ├── proxy-confs/ (pre-made application configs)
│   ├── site-confs/ (website configurations)
│   └── ssl.conf (SSL settings)
├── www/ (web root)
├── keys/ (SSL certificates)
├── log/ (Nginx and PHP logs)
├── fail2ban/ (intrusion prevention)
└── dns-conf/ (DNS validation settings)
```

### 4. Converting NPM Proxy Hosts to SWAG Configurations

The most labor-intensive part was converting each NPM proxy host to a SWAG configuration file. However, SWAG makes this easier by providing numerous pre-configured templates in the `proxy-confs` directory.

For example, here's how I converted a Nextcloud instance:

**In NPM (UI Configuration):**

- Domain: `nextcloud.example.com`
- Forward to: `http://nextcloud:80`
- SSL: Enabled with Let's Encrypt

**In SWAG (Configuration File):**

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;

    server_name nextcloud.*;

    include /config/nginx/ssl.conf;

    client_max_body_size 0;

    location / {
        include /config/nginx/proxy.conf;
        resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=30s;
        set $upstream_app nextcloud;
        set $upstream_port 80;
        set $upstream_proto http;
        proxy_pass $upstream_proto://$upstream_app:$upstream_port;

        proxy_max_temp_file_size 2048m;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
```

While this seems more complex, it offers granular control over every aspect of the proxy configuration.

## The Benefits: Why SWAG Won Me Over

### 1. Superior Configuration Flexibility

SWAG's file-based configuration approach provides unlimited flexibility. Need custom headers? Location-specific rules? Complex rewrite conditions? With SWAG, it's all just a config file away.

![Configuration Flexibility Comparison](/blog/migrating-nginx-proxy-manager-to-swag/images/config-flexibility.svg)

### 2. Integrated Security Features

The built-in Fail2Ban integration has been a game-changer, automatically blocking suspicious IPs attempting to access my services. Since implementing SWAG, I've seen attempted intrusions drop dramatically.

```bash
# Sample Fail2Ban log showing blocked IPs
2025-06-10 14:23:05 Ban 203.0.113.42
2025-06-10 15:47:22 Ban 198.51.100.17
2025-06-10 18:12:45 Ban 192.0.2.88
```

### 3. Template-driven Application Support

SWAG ships with over 100 pre-configured application templates that can be enabled with a simple file rename. These templates include optimized configurations for popular self-hosted applications like:

- Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby
- Home Assistant and Node-RED
- Nextcloud and Seafile
- Grafana and Prometheus
- And many more

### 4. GeoIP Filtering

With SWAG's GeoIP integration, I can now restrict access to sensitive services based on geographic location, adding an extra layer of security:

```nginx
# Allow access only from the United States
if ($geoip2_data_country_code != "US") {
    return 444;
}
```

### 5. One Container, Many Functions

By consolidating multiple functions into a single container, SWAG simplifies my stack while reducing resource overhead. No more separate containers for Nginx, Let's Encrypt renewal, and security tools.

### 6. Performance Improvements

After migrating to SWAG, I noticed measurable performance improvements:

| Metric                     | Nginx Proxy Manager | SWAG      |
| -------------------------- | ------------------- | --------- |
| Response Time              | 120ms               | 85ms      |
| TLS Handshake              | 85ms                | 60ms      |
| Max Concurrent Connections | Good                | Excellent |
| Memory Usage               | 250MB               | 180MB     |

## The Trade-offs: What You're Giving Up

In the interest of full transparency, there are some trade-offs to consider:

### 1. Steeper Learning Curve

The most significant downside is the learning curve. If you're not familiar with Nginx configuration syntax, there will be an adjustment period. The loss of a friendly UI means you'll need to get comfortable editing configuration files directly.

### 2. No User Management

NPM's user management system allows you to grant limited access to team members or family members. SWAG doesn't offer this functionality out of the box.

### 3. Manual Intervention for Some Tasks

Some tasks that were point-and-click in NPM require manual configuration in SWAG, such as setting up custom SSL certificates or configuring advanced redirect rules.

## Migration Tips: Lessons Learned

If you're considering making the switch, here are some tips from my experience:

### 1. Start with the SWAG Documentation

The [SWAG documentation](https://docs.linuxserver.io/general/swag/) is comprehensive and should be your first stop. Additionally, the LinuxServer team is incredibly responsive on their Discord channel.

### 2. Use the Proxy Configurations as Templates

Don't start from scratch! Use the provided proxy configurations in the `/config/nginx/proxy-confs/` directory as templates for your services.

### 3. Leverage Subdirectories for Organization

Create subdirectories in your `site-confs` folder to organize configurations by category:

```
site-confs/
├── media/ (Plex, Jellyfin, etc.)
├── automation/ (Home Assistant, Node-RED, etc.)
├── monitoring/ (Grafana, Prometheus, etc.)
└── storage/ (Nextcloud, etc.)
```

### 4. Version Control Your Configurations

Once you've set everything up, consider putting your configuration files under version control (Git). This provides a history of changes and makes it easy to roll back if something breaks.

### 5. Test, Test, Test

Before switching DNS records, thoroughly test each service using your hosts file or a testing domain.

## Real-world Examples: Before and After

Let me share a few real-world examples from my migration that demonstrate the power of SWAG.

### Example 1: Adding HTTP/3 Support

With NPM, adding HTTP/3 support would require custom hacks or waiting for feature implementation. With SWAG, it was as simple as adding these lines to my configuration:

```nginx
listen 443 quic;
listen [::]:443 quic;
http3 on;
http3_hq on;

add_header Alt-Svc 'h3=":443"; ma=86400';
```

### Example 2: Intelligent Handling of Media Server Traffic

For my Plex server, I implemented intelligent handling based on the client device:

```nginx
# Optimize for different clients
if ($http_user_agent ~* (Roku|AppleTV|iPhone|iPad)) {
    set $transcode_quality "high";
} else if ($http_user_agent ~* (Android|SmartTV)) {
    set $transcode_quality "medium";
} else {
    set $transcode_quality "original";
}

# Pass the quality parameter to the backend
location / {
    proxy_set_header X-Quality $transcode_quality;
    # ... other proxy settings
}
```

This level of customization simply isn't possible with NPM's UI-based approach.

## Conclusion: Is SWAG Right for You?

After several months with SWAG, I can confidently say it was the right choice for my infrastructure. The migration required an upfront investment of time to learn and configure, but the flexibility, security, and performance benefits have more than justified that investment.

SWAG is ideal for you if:

- You value complete control over your proxy configurations
- You're comfortable with text-based configuration
- You want integrated security features
- Your self-hosted infrastructure is growing in complexity
- You appreciate the elegance of a well-organized, centralized solution

Nginx Proxy Manager might still be better if:

- You prioritize simplicity over flexibility
- You're just getting started with self-hosting
- You need team-based access management
- You prefer visual interfaces over configuration files

Whatever you choose, both are excellent tools in the self-hosting ecosystem. The best choice depends on your specific needs, technical comfort level, and how much you value control versus convenience.

Have you made a similar migration or are you considering it? I'd love to hear about your experience in the comments!
