An agent proposes a ticket. The application checks permission and approval, creates it, then loses the response. The agent retries. Does the second attempt create a second ticket?

That question is small enough to test without a model. It is also easy to miss if the only thing you inspect is the final chat response.

I built a small, local harness for the boundary between an agent proposing an action and an application executing it. It has twelve fixtures, a deliberately unsafe mode, and no API keys or external writes. You can download both files and run the same checks.

**This is an educational experiment, not a report from a production deployment or a benchmark of an AI model.** It tests a deterministic action gate. A passing result says that these particular fixtures behave as specified.

## Run the example

Download the [evaluation script](/examples/agent-action-evals/evaluate.mjs) and [test fixtures](/examples/agent-action-evals/cases.json) into the same directory. Read the script, then run it with Node.js:

```sh
node evaluate.mjs
node evaluate.mjs --unsafe
```

The first command should print `12/12 fixtures passed (guarded mode)` and exit successfully. The second deliberately bypasses the gate. It should print `1/12 fixtures passed (unsafe mode)` and exit with code 1. That failure is intentional: it demonstrates that the checks notice missing controls. Both modes write only to an in-memory array.

In this repository, the equivalent command is:

```sh
node public/examples/agent-action-evals/evaluate.mjs
```

## Separate a proposal from permission

The demo accepts one tool: `create_ticket`. Its proposal contains a project, title, and request key. Those fields describe what the agent wants to do; they do not establish its authority to do it.

The application supplies a separate trusted context containing the user identity, allowed projects, and approved actions. In the fixtures, that context is test setup. In a real application, it must come from authenticated application state and the approval workflow, outside the model's control.

```text
Agent proposal
    → validate the tool and arguments
    → check project access
    → require approval for the exact action
    → check the request key
    → execute the permitted fields
```

The ordering matters. A previously completed request does not bypass today's access or approval checks. Extra proposal fields, including `approved: true`, cannot change the trusted context and are never forwarded to the mock tool.

## The twelve fixtures

Each fixture starts with a fresh gate. A retry fixture contains multiple proposals so they share the same in-memory request history.

| Fixture                                        | Expected outcome            | Expected writes   |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Approved action                                | Executed                    | One ticket        |
| Missing approval                               | Approval required           | None              |
| Proposal claims it is approved                 | Approval required           | None              |
| Retrieved text claims approval                 | Approval required           | None              |
| Different project, even with approval          | Forbidden                   | None              |
| Unknown tool                                   | Unsupported tool            | None              |
| Blank title                                    | Invalid                     | None              |
| Title has the wrong type                       | Invalid                     | None              |
| Null proposal                                  | Invalid                     | None              |
| Arguments changed after approval               | Approval required           | None              |
| Same request retried                           | Executed, then duplicate    | One ticket        |
| Same key reused for different approved actions | Executed, then key conflict | First ticket only |

The harness checks both the returned outcomes and the exact writes. Checking only a response such as “approval required” would miss an implementation that rejects the request after it has already changed state.

The unsafe mode still passes the approved-action fixture. It fails the other eleven because it executes proposals without checking permission, approval, or request history. This is a useful negative control; a suite that also passed the unsafe version would deserve immediate suspicion.

## Approval belongs to the exact action

“Allow this tool” and “approve this ticket” are different policies. This example chooses the narrower one: approval covers the tool, project, title, and request key together.

If a proposal changes after approval, it needs a new approval. The changed-arguments fixture proves that an approval for “Investigate timeout” cannot authorize “Delete the audit log,” even though both are merely ticket titles in this simulation.

The fixture that includes a forged instruction in a `document` field checks a similarly narrow property: extra text cannot grant approval through this interface. It does **not** prove a model resists prompt injection. No model reads the document here. Testing the upstream model requires supplying hostile documents to the real workflow and examining the resulting proposals.

## A retry must preserve the identity of the work

The demo scopes its request key to the user and project. When the same key arrives again, it compares the approved action with the recorded one:

- Same key and same action: report a duplicate without another write.
- Same key and different action: report a conflict without another write.

The request key must remain stable across retries. If an agent invents a new key on every attempt, this mechanism cannot recognize duplicate work. A production application should own the logical request identity and carry it through retries.

An in-memory map is enough to demonstrate the policy, but it does not survive restarts or coordinate multiple processes. This example's execution is synchronous. It does not test concurrent requests, a crash between the external write and the local record, or the case where the downstream service succeeds but its response is lost. Those require durable coordination and a recovery design appropriate to the actual service. Do not copy this map into a production integration and call it exactly-once delivery.

## Add the model evaluation as a separate layer

After testing the boundary, I would evaluate whether the real workflow proposes the right actions in the first place. Keep that experiment separate so a permission bug does not get confused with a planning error.

For each task, record the expected outcome, allowed actions, actual tool calls, unintended writes, latency, and cost. Include tasks that should finish without any write. Keep the model version, prompts, tool definitions, and test data fixed when comparing changes; run repeated trials to expose variability.

Report failures by category. A single overall pass rate hides the difference between an agent failing to create a ticket and creating a ticket in a project it should never access. Expand the dataset with independently designed cases and failures found in the real workflow. Twelve hand-written fixtures are a starting point, not a release criterion for every application.

## Where this fits

If you are starting with tool calling, read [the TypeScript MCP server walkthrough](/blog/building-mcp-server-typescript/). For the broader security questions, continue with [agent trust boundaries and MCP](/blog/ai-agents-mcp-security-crisis/).

The useful artifact here is the executable contract: these proposals may create one ticket, and these proposals must create none. That gives the rest of the agent workflow a boundary you can inspect, break deliberately, and improve.

For a broader treatment of task design, graders, and repeated trials, see [Anthropic's guide to agent evaluations](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents).

I read a lot of engineering blogs. Most weeks I open more posts than I finish, and the ones I do finish often leave me with the announcement and not the mechanism. A post says "we cut p99 latency by 40%" and I spend the next twenty minutes reading three other articles to work out what they actually changed.

So I built **[Understory](https://understory.piyushmehta.com/)**. It watches the posts that [engineeringblogs.xyz](https://engineeringblogs.xyz/) already aggregates, and when one looks worth the time it produces an explainer: context, how the thing works, a diagram, an ELI5, the trade-offs the announcement leaves out, and a source behind every substantive claim. A person reviews each one before it goes live.

> **Try it:** [understory.piyushmehta.com](https://understory.piyushmehta.com/). Source on [GitHub](https://github.com/piyush97/understory), code under MIT and content under CC BY 4.0.

The name is the layer of a forest that sits under the canopy. The headline is the canopy. The interesting part is underneath it.

## What a reader gets

Each explainer is written for a senior engineer at a different company who wants to use the idea in their own work. The goal is that you can explain the post's mechanism to a colleague without reading anything else first.

![An Understory explainer page with a large headline, a dek, the source publisher, and a TL;DR card beside a sheet record](/blog/understory-engineering-blogs-explained/images/explainer.png)

A page has a fixed shape:

- a context headline and a one-sentence summary, so you know in five seconds whether to keep going;
- a TL;DR of two to five points;
- background and mechanism sections that separate the author's findings from general knowledge;
- a diagram rendered from validated data;
- an ELI5 with a `limit` field that says where the analogy breaks;
- trade-offs, when the idea is useful, and caveats;
- numbered sources, with every citation in the text pointing to one of them.

There are no accounts, comments, or votes, and no "chat with this article." Bookmarks live in your browser. The public site is read-only and fully server-rendered, and a reader request never waits on a model.

## The pipeline is deliberately boring

I wanted something I could leave running without worrying about it. Every step is a separate job with its own row in the database, so a failure stops at the step that failed and nothing half-finished leaks onto the site.

![Understory's six-step pipeline: Discover, Extract, Draft, Validate, Review, Publish](/blog/understory-engineering-blogs-explained/images/pipeline.png)

1. **Discover.** A cron trigger runs every 15 minutes, reads the engineeringblogs.xyz listing, and records new links. It takes at most six new posts per run, ignores anything older than four days, and skips sources under 220 words.
2. **Extract.** A queue job fetches the article and runs it through Cloudflare's `HTMLRewriter`. It strips navigation, share bars, comments, and ads, finds the main content, and stores a snapshot of up to 220 blocks with a content hash. Each block keeps its heading path, which makes citations precise later.
3. **Draft.** A second job asks Workers AI (`@cf/qwen/qwen3-30b-a3b-fp8`) for a structured explanation using `response_format: json_schema`.
4. **Validate.** The draft must pass a Zod schema and a second round of semantic checks before it can enter the review queue.
5. **Review.** I read the draft against the snapshot and approve or reject it, with a note.
6. **Publish.** Approval writes an immutable revision. Fixing a published explainer means publishing a new revision; the old one never changes in place.

## Two Workers, one database, zero dollars

The whole thing runs on Cloudflare's free plan. That was a hard constraint from the start, and it shaped most of the design.

![Understory architecture: a reader and editor hit understory-web; understory-pipeline is driven by a cron trigger and a queue, fetches engineeringblogs.xyz and publisher pages, calls Workers AI, and writes drafts to a shared D1 database](/blog/understory-engineering-blogs-explained/images/architecture.png)

`understory-web` is a Hono app with server-rendered JSX. It serves the public pages, a JSON API, RSS and a sitemap, and the private editorial desk. `understory-pipeline` handles the cron, the queue consumer, extraction, generation, and validation. They share one D1 database that holds articles, snapshots, revisions, reviews, jobs, and the AI budget.

The repo also has an [interactive version](https://github.com/piyush97/understory/blob/main/docs/architecture.html) of that diagram, built with Archify, with route focus and source links.

## What validation checks

LLMs produce plausible JSON easily. Producing JSON where every reference resolves is harder, so the schema only gets a draft halfway there. After Zod passes, `validateExplanation` checks the things a type system can't:

- every `cite` in a paragraph, list item, ELI5 block, diagram node, or diagram edge must point to a source that exists;
- every source URL must parse as `http:` or `https:`;
- source, section, and node ids must be unique;
- every diagram edge must connect two nodes that exist, and no edge may loop back to the node it starts from;
- a sequence diagram needs at least one message.

Generated prose can't contain links at all. Inline runs may carry a citation id, code, bold, or italics, and URLs live only in the sources list. That one rule closes off a whole class of problems where a model invents a plausible-looking link.

If validation fails, the pipeline retries once, sending back up to 24 specific issues and the first 8,000 characters of the previous output. If the second attempt fails too, the draft stays in the job table with its errors. It never shows up on the site.

The system prompt pushes the same way. It tells the model to lead with the mechanism, treat vendor benchmarks as claims, never invent URLs, numbers, quotes, or people, never copy a source sentence longer than twelve words, and say so in the caveats when a source is thin or promotional.

## Diagrams come from data

I didn't want the model drawing SVG. It returns a small graph (two to ten nodes, up to sixteen edges, flow or sequence) and a deterministic renderer in `src/domain/diagram.ts` does the layout.

Flow diagrams get a topological sort into columns. If a cycle slips through, the leftover nodes go into a final column instead of crashing. Nodes have fixed sizes and coordinates are rounded. Element ids come from an FNV-1a hash of the title and description, so the same input always produces byte-identical SVG. Each figure ships with `role="group"`, a `<title>`, and a `<desc>` so screen readers get the same explanation as everyone else.

Each node and edge can also carry its own citation, which is why the figures on Understory show small `s1` markers. You can trace a box in the diagram back to the paragraph in the original post that justifies it.

## Spending a free AI budget without overspending it

Workers AI's free tier gives you 10,000 neurons a day. Understory budgets 8,000 by default and caps the setting at 9,000, so there's always headroom.

Every generation attempt reserves an estimated 500 neurons before calling the model, in a single atomic statement:

```sql
INSERT INTO ai_budget (day, reserved_neurons, used_neurons, generations, updated_at)
SELECT ?, ?, 0, 1, ? WHERE ? <= ?
ON CONFLICT (day) DO UPDATE SET
  reserved_neurons = reserved_neurons + excluded.reserved_neurons,
  generations = generations + 1,
  updated_at = excluded.updated_at
WHERE ai_budget.reserved_neurons + ai_budget.used_neurons + excluded.reserved_neurons <= ?
```

If the row would go over budget, nothing changes and the job is deferred to the next UTC midnight. If the call fails because of a network or binding error, the reservation is released, because a transport failure shouldn't eat the day's budget. The API doesn't report exact neuron usage, so a completed attempt is recorded at the conservative estimate.

Reading the site never touches this path. If the budget runs out, the index keeps serving; it just stops growing until tomorrow.

## Leases, so a retry can't overwrite newer work

Queues retry. Workers get evicted. On the free tier you assume both will happen. Every pipeline job holds a lease token, and every write the pipeline makes is conditional on still holding that lease. Generation renews its lease before each attempt and quits with "Job lease lost." if another worker has taken over.

State transitions go through `db.batch`, so a job is never half-moved.

## Caching without purges

Pages are cached with the Cache API, using TTLs from 120 seconds for the index up to 900 seconds for topics, sources, and about. The cache key includes `__v=<publicationVersion>`.

Approving a draft increments that publication version in the same batch that writes the revision. Every cached page is now addressed by a key that doesn't exist yet, so the next request renders fresh. There's no purge API call to forget and no partial invalidation to debug.

## Being a good citizen to publishers

Understory reads other people's work, so it needed to be careful about it:

- Outbound fetches block private and reserved IP ranges and local-style hostnames, follow redirects manually with a cap, and enforce a timeout and a byte limit. There's no arbitrary URL ingestion and no open proxy.
- The bot identifies itself as `UnderstoryBot` with a link back to the about page.
- Original publishers and authors are linked prominently on every explainer, and "Read original" is the primary button.
- Public snapshots keep only two or three short quotations per source.

## The editorial desk

Every draft passes a person before it's published. The desk shows the draft as a reader would see it, next to a record of the article, the snapshot id, the model, the prompt version, and the schema version.

![The Understory editorial desk showing a draft explainer beside its draft record, an approve button, and a reject form](/blog/understory-engineering-blogs-explained/images/admin-review.png)

Access is a bearer token compared via SHA-256 digests, and optionally a Cloudflare Access JWT that the Worker verifies itself: RS256 keys fetched from the team's certs endpoint, with issuer, audience, `exp`, and `nbf` checked. The Worker doesn't trust that the edge did it.

## The drawing-sheet design

The visual design borrows from technical drawing sheets: paper-coloured background, a faint grid, red-pen accents, figures presented as numbered plates. Barlow Condensed for display, Source Serif 4 for reading, Spline Sans Mono for metadata, all self-hosted. Dark mode follows your system.

I wanted the index to be dense, like Hacker News, and the article page to read like a teaching document. Topic filters and a publisher index cover browsing; everything else stays out of the way.

## What I'd tell you if you built one

- Make the model decide less. It writes prose and returns a small graph. Ordinary code does layout, linking, validation, and publishing.
- Check references as well as shape. Zod tells you the JSON is well formed. Your own checks tell you it's true to itself.
- Put the budget in the database. A conditional insert is a perfectly good rate limiter.
- Keep a person in the loop where it's cheap. Reading a draft that already passed validation is quick. Retracting a wrong explanation is not.

## Go read something

Understory launched today with eleven explainers across AI infrastructure, networking, databases, security, observability, and more. New ones show up as the pipeline finds posts worth explaining and I approve them.

- Read it at [understory.piyushmehta.com](https://understory.piyushmehta.com/)
- Follow the RSS feed like any other blog.
- Fork it from [github.com/piyush97/understory](https://github.com/piyush97/understory). It deploys to a free Cloudflare account.

If a post you care about deserves an explainer, or one gets something wrong, open an issue on the repo. I'd much rather fix a revision than leave a bad one up.

Create your own website monitor in seconds!

### Step 1

Create a new repository, I'll name it piyushmehta.com

### Step 2

Create a directory named and workflows inside it `.github/workflows`

### Step 3

Create a file with any name, I'll name is `uptime-monitor.yml`

### Step 4

Write the following in uptime-monitor.yaml

```yml
name: Uptime Monitor

on:
  schedule:
    # Run every hour, You can choose your custom time
    - cron: '*/60 *  * * *'

jobs:
  ping_site:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    name: Uptime Check
    steps:
      - name: Ping Site
        uses: srt32/uptime@v0.2
        with:
          url-to-hit: 'https://piyushmehta.com/' # Website whose uptime you want to track
          expected-statuses: '200'
```

> Whenever your website is down, you'll get a notification from GitHub.

Fin!

This site ran on Vercel for years without much drama. Then I moved it to Cloudflare Workers, and for about a day, every link I shared to a new post rendered as a blank blue rectangle. Not broken in an obvious way: the request came back `200 OK`, the content type was `image/png`, the dimensions were exactly right. There was just nothing on it. No title, no text, nothing.

That single bug turned into the best possible tour of what actually changes when you move a site off a Node.js serverless platform and onto a V8 isolate. This is the record of what moved, what broke, and why.

> **The short version:** the adapter swap was the easy part. The hard part was a native Rust binary that only works at build time now, and a caching layer that kept an old broken image alive long after the underlying bug was fixed.

## Why leave Vercel at all

Nothing was on fire. The honest reason is that I wanted one platform instead of two: Cloudflare already sat in front of DNS and a couple of other side projects, and running the actual site somewhere else meant a second dashboard, a second set of environment variables, and a second mental model for "how does a request get served." Workers also don't have the cold-start-after-idle behavior that Vercel's regional functions do, and I liked the idea of the site living on Cloudflare's edge network instead of one region. None of that is a knock on Vercel. It's a genuinely good platform, and this migration was about consolidation, not escaping something broken.

## The adapter swap

The actual config change is small. `astro.config.mjs` went from the Vercel adapter to the Cloudflare one:

```diff
-import vercel from '@astrojs/vercel';
+import cloudflare from '@astrojs/cloudflare';

-adapter: vercel({
-  webAnalytics: { enabled: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' },
-  imageService: true,
-  isr: { expiration: 60 * 60 * 24 },
-}),
+adapter: cloudflare({
+  imageService: { build: 'compile', runtime: 'passthrough' },
+  prerenderEnvironment: 'node',
+}),
```

Vercel's ISR (incremental static regeneration) doesn't have a Cloudflare equivalent, so that config just disappears: pages are either prerendered at build time or served on demand from the Worker, with no middle ground where a page gets cached and silently regenerated later. A new `wrangler.jsonc` shows up alongside it, describing the Worker itself: the entrypoint, the assets binding, and (this detail mattered more than it looked like it would) where the static output actually lives.

```jsonc
{
  "main": "@astrojs/cloudflare/entrypoints/server",
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"],
  "assets": { "binding": "ASSETS", "directory": "./dist" },
}
```

Where Vercel produced one build output, Cloudflare produces two: `dist/client` for everything Workers Assets serves directly, and `dist/server` for the actual Worker script. The CI build-verification step had to change to match, because checking for a single `dist` directory was no longer enough to know the build actually worked:

```diff
-[ -d "dist" ] && echo "Build directory exists" || exit 1
+[ -d "dist/client" ] || { echo "Static asset output missing"; exit 1; }
+[ -f "dist/server/entry.mjs" ] || { echo "Worker entrypoint missing"; exit 1; }
```

## Redis had to get edge-native too

The post-reactions endpoint uses Upstash Redis, and the default `@upstash/redis` client assumes a Node.js runtime; it isn't guaranteed to work inside a Worker's fetch-based environment. Upstash ships a dedicated entrypoint for exactly this:

```diff
-import { Redis } from '@upstash/redis';
+import { Redis } from '@upstash/redis/cloudflare';

 const redis = new Redis({
   url,
   token,
+  signal: () => AbortSignal.timeout(2500),
+  retry: { retries: 1, backoff: (retryCount) => retryCount * 50 },
 });
```

I also added an explicit timeout and a single retry. Vercel's regional functions had generous defaults that papered over slow Redis round-trips; a Worker doesn't, so an unbounded request is a much easier way to leave a user staring at a spinner.

The rate limiter's IP detection flipped order too. On Vercel, `clientAddress` was the trustworthy source. On Cloudflare, it's `cf-connecting-ip`, set by Cloudflare's own edge and not forwardable by the client, with `x-forwarded-for` kept only as a last-resort fallback:

```diff
 const ip =
-  clientAddress ||
   request.headers.get('cf-connecting-ip') ||
+  clientAddress ||
   request.headers.get('x-forwarded-for')?.split(',')[0].trim() ||
   'anonymous';
```

Get this ordering wrong on a rate limiter and it isn't a cosmetic bug. It's a rate limiter a client can bypass by setting its own `x-forwarded-for` header.

## The bug that actually cost me a day

This site generates its own Open Graph images (the cards you see when a link gets shared on LinkedIn or X) using [Satori](https://github.com/vercel/satori) to lay out a React-ish element tree as SVG, then [`@resvg/resvg-js`](https://github.com/thx/resvg-js) to rasterize that SVG to a PNG. `resvg-js` is a Rust library exposed to Node through a native addon. That's fine in a Node.js serverless function. It is not fine in a Worker: a V8 isolate has no filesystem and can't load a compiled native binary.

![Two lanes: a build machine where a native Rust binary runs freely and bakes static PNGs, versus a Cloudflare Worker where the same binary cannot execute and a silent fallback renders a blank card](/blog/vercel-to-cloudflare-migration/images/build-vs-worker.svg)

So every OG-image route had to move from generating an image per request (`prerender = false`, fine on Vercel) to generating every possible image once, at build time, via `getStaticPaths` (`prerender = true`, the only thing that works on Workers). That's the right fix, and by itself it's not even a hard one.

The actual bug was subtler, and it's the reason this took a day instead of an hour. The font file was being resolved with `path.join(process.cwd(), 'InterVariable.ttf')`, a path that happens to work when you run `node` from the project root and does not reliably resolve to the same place inside a build runner's working directory. When the font failed to load, the code didn't throw. It fell through to a fallback renderer that draws the card with plain SVG `<text>` and no font attached, which resvg silently renders as nothing. Correct dimensions, correct content type, `200 OK`, and zero visible pixels of text: a blank blue card that looks, to any monitoring you might have, like a complete success.

The fix was to resolve the font relative to the module's own file instead of the process's working directory, and to give the fallback path an explicit, always-available font so it can never again silently render invisible text. But by the time that shipped, the damage was already cached: LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord had all fetched the blank version and stored it under an image URL that never changes. Fixing the renderer doesn't un-cache anything on someone else's server. I ended up building a whole second layer on top of the fix just for that: a content-hash query parameter on every card URL so the URL itself changes when the card does, plus a manifest so a page can never again advertise a card that was never actually generated, plus a build step that walks every rendered HTML page and fails the build if a single `og:image` doesn't resolve to a real, correctly sized PNG.

## What I'd do differently

Two things, if I were starting this migration over.

First, I'd audit every dependency for native bindings before touching the adapter, not after the blank cards showed up. `@resvg/resvg-js` was the only one in this codebase, and it's exactly the kind of dependency that keeps working right up until the moment your architecture changes underneath it. Nothing about "it built successfully in CI" tells you whether it'll run in the target runtime.

Second, I'd write the build-time coverage check first, not as a response to a production bug. It's about forty lines of Node that walk the built output and confirm every generated asset a page claims to have actually exists on disk. It would have caught the missing-card class of bug on the very first build, instead of after a report from someone whose link preview looked broken.

If you're mid-migration on something similar, this is the pattern I'd watch for: it's rarely the framework config that bites you. It's the dependency you forgot was doing something clever behind a "just works" abstraction.

One of my 12TB Seagate IronWolf drives developed 52 bad sectors. At that point, about 3.4TB of homelab data was depending on the surviving half of my ZFS mirror. The Proxmox server stayed online. My media and application data remained available, Seagate replaced the failed drive without hassle, and ZFS rebuilt the mirror onto a new 16TB IronWolf. This is the sequence I followed, including the USB enclosure reset that briefly suspended the pool and the checksum errors ZFS caught after a later reboot. ZFS could not stop the drive from failing. It did stop that failure from deleting my data. ## TL;DR: the recovery in numbers - Failed disk: 12TB Seagate IronWolf with 52 bad sectors - Data at risk: 3.37TiB allocated on a degraded ZFS mirror - Warranty replacement: new 16TB Seagate IronWolf - Resilver: 3.38TiB in 5 hours 30 minutes - Resilver result: zero errors and the mirror returned `ONLINE` - Usable capacity: still 10.9TiB because the other mirror member is 12TB The mirror supplied another copy, ZFS checked the blocks, and Seagate supplied the replacement drive. ## My Proxmox ZFS mirror before the failure My `vault` pool lives on a Proxmox server. It stores media, application configuration, and other homelab data. I built it as a two-drive ZFS mirror: ```text vault └── mirror-0 ├── 12TB IronWolf └── 12TB IronWolf ``` Both drives sit in a TerraMaster USB DAS. The enclosure exposes each disk to ZFS instead of hiding them behind hardware RAID. ZFS needs that direct access to manage the mirror and verify checksums. The pool held about 3.37TiB of allocated data when I replaced the drive. A mirror gets the capacity of its smallest member, with another copy of each block on the other disk. When one drive started failing, that second copy kept the pool alive. ## The 12TB IronWolf had 52 bad sectors SMART showed 52 bad sectors on one of the 12TB drives. I was not going to clear the warning and keep using it. Once a disk cannot reliably read its own sectors, I do not want it holding the only copy of anything. I removed it from service and opened a Seagate warranty claim. The process was painless, and Seagate honored the warranty. They sent a 16TB Seagate IronWolf to replace the failed 12TB drive. The replacement arrived with the clean baseline I wanted: ```text SMART overall health: PASSED Power-on hours: 0 Reallocated sectors: 0 Current pending sectors: 0 Offline uncorrectable: 0 Reported uncorrectable: 0 Command timeouts: 0 Interface CRC errors: 0 ``` Its short SMART self-test also completed without error. The Seagate part was refreshingly easy. A failed drive already gives you enough to worry about. I did not have to fight the warranty process too. ## The degraded mirror kept serving data After I removed the failed disk, ZFS showed the pool as `DEGRADED`: ```text pool: vault state: DEGRADED mirror-0 missing UNAVAIL survivor ONLINE ``` The warning was serious. The pool had no redundancy left, so another disk failure would have meant data loss. The datasets were still available from the surviving member. The disk had failed, the mirror had lost redundancy, and ZFS made both facts obvious without taking my data offline. ## Hot-plugging the replacement reset the USB enclosure The recovery got more stressful when I inserted the 16TB drive. The TerraMaster enclosure reset its shared USB connection, and the surviving 12TB disk disappeared for a moment. ZFS suspended the pool: ```text pool: vault state: SUSPENDED ``` That was the right response. With its only available member temporarily gone, ZFS stopped accepting I/O rather than claiming that writes had succeeded. Once both disks were visible again, I checked their model, serial, WWN, SMART state, and partition signatures. Then I resumed the pool: ```bash zpool clear vault ``` The pool returned to `DEGRADED` with the surviving member online. `zpool clear` removed the suspended state. It did not restore redundancy. This incident also exposed a weakness in my setup. Both mirrored disks share the same enclosure, cable, controller, and power supply. The mirror protects against one disk failing, but those shared components can still affect both drives at once. ## The replacement command was `zpool replace` The 16TB disk had to replace the missing mirror member. Adding it as another top-level vdev would have changed the pool topology instead of repairing the mirror. `zpool add` was the wrong command for this job. I used: ```bash zpool replace vault \ \ /dev/disk/by-id/wwn- ``` The WWN path under `/dev/disk/by-id/` identifies the physical disk. I did not use `/dev/sdc` because Linux can assign a different device letter after a reboot or USB reconnect. ZFS partitioned the blank replacement and started resilvering it. ## ZFS resilvered 3.38TiB with zero errors The resilver copied the allocated data from the surviving 12TB drive to the new 16TB drive: ```text scan: resilvered 3.38T in 05:30:27 with 0 errors state: ONLINE errors: No known data errors ``` Both drives finished online. ZFS recorded zero read, write, and checksum errors during the resilver. The datasets mounted normally, Proxmox reported the storage entries as active, and the pool had redundancy again. Usable capacity remains about 10.9TiB. The smaller member limits a mirror, so the extra space on the 16TB disk cannot be used yet. If I eventually replace the remaining 12TB drive with another 16TB or larger disk, the mirror can expand. I would rather have redundancy now than extra capacity I cannot safely use. ## ZFS caught 11 checksum mismatches after reboot A later Proxmox reboot imported the pool and recorded 11 checksum mismatches on the new member. The pool remained `ONLINE`, and applications were unaffected because the other mirror member had a valid copy. ZFS compared the data with its stored checksum, rejected the incorrect bytes, and read the correct copy from the other disk. The surrounding hardware evidence remained clean. SMART passed, the reallocated, pending, and uncorrectable sector counts stayed at zero, and the interface CRC count did not increase. The kernel showed no new USB reset or I/O failure, and ZFS reported no known data errors. A full scrub began checking every allocated block. I am keeping the checksum counters until it finishes because clearing them now would discard useful evidence. If the scrub finishes cleanly and the count stays at 11, I can clear the historical device errors. If the count keeps rising, I will investigate the TerraMaster bay, USB bridge, cable, power delivery, and the replacement drive. I liked seeing ZFS do what I had set it up to do. A successful read was not enough. The bytes also had to match. ## What ZFS and the mirror each did The mirror and ZFS handled different parts of the failure. ### The mirror kept another copy The surviving disk still contained the pool after the first drive became untrustworthy. Later, when one copy failed a checksum, the mirror gave ZFS another copy to read. Checksums can detect bad data, but they cannot recreate the correct bytes. That requires redundancy or a backup. ### ZFS checked the data ZFS checksums data and metadata. It can tell the difference between a drive returning data and a drive returning the correct data. During a scrub, ZFS checks allocated blocks and repairs a bad copy when another valid copy exists. ### ZFS made the failures visible `DEGRADED` told me the pool had lost redundancy. `SUSPENDED` stopped I/O when the only available member vanished during the USB reset. Neither state was pleasant, but neither hid the problem. ### Stable disk IDs kept me on the right drive The WWN path kept pointing to the replacement even when `/dev/sda`, `/dev/sdb`, and `/dev/sdc` changed after reconnects and reboots. A filesystem cannot protect you if you run the right command against the wrong disk. ## What I will keep doing ### RAID is not a backup The mirror protected me from one disk failure. It would not protect me from accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, a destructive command, or corruption copied to both members. Anything irreplaceable still needs an independent backup. ### Run scrubs and read the result A scrub verifies data while another copy is available for repair. I care whether it repaired anything, found permanent errors, or caused a device counter to increase, not only whether the scheduled job ran. ### Use SMART and ZFS together SMART identified the original failing drive and gave me a hardware baseline for the replacement. The later checksum events showed why filesystem checks still matter. A drive can report healthy while ZFS detects incorrect data. ### Use `/dev/disk/by-id/` Device letters are convenient labels, not stable identities. Replacement commands should use persistent disk IDs. ### Treat the enclosure as shared hardware Hot-plugging one bay reset the USB path for both disks. The enclosure, USB controller, cable, and power supply need the same attention as the drives. ### Check the pool topology before changing it `zpool replace` repairs a missing mirror member. `zpool add` changes the topology. I checked the command and target before pressing Enter. ## Frequently asked questions ### Can ZFS recover from a failed drive? Yes, if the pool still has a valid copy. One member of my two-disk mirror failed, while the other kept the pool available. I replaced the missing member and ZFS resilvered the allocated data onto it. A single-disk ZFS pool can detect corruption with checksums, but it has no second copy to repair from. ### Is a ZFS mirror the same as RAID 1? Both provide two-copy redundancy. ZFS also manages the filesystem, block checksums, scrubs, repairs, snapshots, and the pool itself. When two copies disagree, ZFS can verify which one matches the stored checksum and repair the other. ### Does a 12TB + 16TB ZFS mirror provide 28TB? No. The smallest member limits the mirror. My 12TB + 16TB mirror remains about 10.9TiB usable. Replacing the remaining 12TB disk with another 16TB or larger drive will allow the mirror to expand. ### Does ZFS or RAID replace a backup? No. My mirror handled one disk failure. It cannot protect both copies from deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a destructive command. Irreplaceable data still needs an independent backup. ### Should I use `zpool add` when replacing a failed mirror disk? No. `zpool add` changes the pool topology. Use `zpool replace` with the missing vdev and the replacement disk's stable `/dev/disk/by-id/` path. ## The recovery was boring, which is what I wanted The working sequence was straightforward: 1. identify the failing disk; 2. keep the degraded pool stable; 3. get the warranty replacement; 4. verify its identity and SMART baseline; 5. replace the missing vdev by stable ID; 6. monitor the resilver until it finishes; and 7. check the pool, datasets, mounts, and disk health afterward. Seagate honored the warranty without hassle. ZFS and the mirror kept the drive failure from becoming a data-loss event. The drive failed, I replaced it, and my data stayed put. That is what I wanted when I built the mirror.
